Part I · Why the web needs an agent interface

Chapter 1: The Agentic Web Arrives

“We view browser-using AI as inevitable: so much work happens in browsers that giving Claude the ability to see what you’re looking at, click buttons, and fill forms will make it substantially more useful.”

— Anthropic, “Piloting Claude in Chrome”1

A tent, a deadline and a very patient robot

Lars has a hiking trip in Jotunheimen in three weeks and no tent. On Tuesday night he opens Trailhead, a Norwegian outdoor-gear store, and instead of clicking through it himself he types into his browser’s assistant panel: “Find me a two-person tent under 4,000 kroner that’s in stock, compare the two best-rated ones, and put the better one in my cart.” Then he goes to make tea.

The assistant gets to work the only way most of today’s agents can. It takes a screenshot of the Trailhead homepage and sends it to a model, together with a snapshot of the page’s structure. The model decides that the magnifying-glass icon is probably search, so the agent clicks it and types “tent”. Another screenshot. The results page has a filter sidebar: a price slider, a “Capacity” accordion that starts collapsed, and an “In stock only” toggle styled as a little pill. The agent drags the slider, overshoots, takes another screenshot, reads the label (“0 – 4 350 kr”), and nudges it back. It opens the accordion, ticks “2 persons”, and waits while the product grid reloads. On the first attempt it reads the grid before the new results arrive and starts comparing tents that are no longer on the page.

Eventually it opens two product pages in turn, scrolls each one to find the specifications table, copies weights and pack sizes out of the pixels, and picks a winner. On the product page it meets a size selector, a colour swatch and a quantity stepper. It chooses “Moss”, clicks “Add to cart”, and a slide-in drawer appears, offering a matching footprint at 20 per cent off. Is that a confirmation, or an upsell that needs dismissing before the cart updates? The agent takes another screenshot and thinks about it.

By the time Lars comes back with his tea, the job is done, probably. It took dozens of model calls, a minute or two of wall-clock time, and a fair amount of luck. If Trailhead had shipped a redesign that afternoon, or if the filter sidebar had loaded a little more slowly, the agent might have put the wrong tent in the cart, or no tent at all, and neither Lars nor Trailhead would have known why.

This chapter is about that gap: between what browser agents are already being asked to do and the way they currently have to do it. It explains what browser agents are, how they operate websites today, where that approach breaks, what it costs, and why the website, not only the agent, has a stake in fixing it. It ends by introducing the projects you will build throughout the book and by setting out what the book covers and what it does not.

Agents in the browser

The WebMCP specification starts its terminology section with a definition worth borrowing. An agent is “an autonomous assistant that can understand a user’s goals and take actions on the user’s behalf to achieve them.” Today, it adds, these are typically built on large language model (LLM) platforms “interacting with users via text-based chat interfaces.”2 What makes an agent a browser agent is where it acts. The spec defines a browser agent as an agent “provided by or through the browser that could be built directly into the browser or hosted by it, for example, via an extension or plug-in.”2:1

Two years ago, that would have been a description of a research demo. By the autumn of 2026 it describes products that millions of people can install. They come in three broad shapes, distinguished by where the agent lives relative to the page it acts on (Figure 1.1).

Built into the browser

The most visible shape is the assistant that ships with the browser. In September 2025, Google announced that Gemini in Chrome would act as “an AI browsing assistant”, and said it was developing “more advanced agentic capabilities for Gemini in Chrome that can perform multi-step tasks for you from start to finish, like ordering groceries.” Its stated ambition was to turn “30-minute chores into 3-click user journeys.”3 OpenAI went further and built a whole browser around its assistant. It introduced ChatGPT Atlas in October 2025 as “a new web browser built with ChatGPT at its core,” with an agent mode in which “ChatGPT may ask you if it should start opening tabs and clicking in your browser to complete the task.”4 Atlas didn’t last. OpenAI’s help centre now says it “has been retired and no longer receives updates,”5 which is as good a reminder as any of how quickly this landscape moves. Perplexity markets its Comet browser, available on desktop and mobile, as “the browser that works for you”.6

These assistants have a privileged position. They can see every tab, they share the user’s signed-in sessions, and the browser vendor controls the whole stack, from the side panel to the model.

Extensions

The second shape is the agent that arrives as a browser extension. Anthropic’s Claude in Chrome is the clearest example. It began in August 2025 as a research preview for 1,000 users, “a Claude extension for Chrome where trusted users can instruct Claude to take actions on their behalf within the browser,” and by December 2025 it was available on all of Anthropic’s paid plans.1:1 Extensions are how agent makers who don’t own a browser get into one. They are also how developers build their own agents. Chrome’s WebMCP documentation offers two extensions for exactly that purpose, an example agent and a tool inspector, and it notes plainly that “Chrome Extensions can query and execute WebMCP tools with content scripts.”7

A close cousin is the agent that runs a browser on your behalf somewhere else. OpenAI’s Operator drove a remote browser in the cloud that the user could take over at any point, and it was folded into ChatGPT as “ChatGPT agent” in July 2025.8 The browser is no longer the one on your desk, but the technique for operating websites is the same, and so are its problems.

In the page

The third shape is easy to overlook: an agent that a website ships inside itself. A support assistant in the corner of a SaaS dashboard, a shopping helper on a store’s product pages, a copilot inside a document editor. These agents are part of the site, or embedded in it from a third party, and they act on the page from within. The WebMCP explainer counts them explicitly: tools “can be invoked by AI agents, including those built into the browser, hosted in iframes, or running in extensions.”9 A page-embedded agent can even run its model on the user’s device. Chrome’s Prompt API exposes Gemini Nano, a model that runs locally in the browser, and needs no network connection after its first download.10 Chapter 7 builds an agent of this kind, and the book’s Test Agent project uses the same idea to exercise tools.

All three shapes share one constraint. Whoever built the agent, it ends up in front of a web page that was designed for people, and it has to work out how to use it.

Actuation: using the web like a person

Chrome’s documentation has a name for how agents do that today: actuation, “the act of an agent simulating manual mouse clicks and text input, as though it were the human user engaging with your website.”7:1 The WebMCP explainer describes the same technique from the agent’s side. General-purpose agents “often rely on observing the browser state through a combination of screenshots, and DOM and accessibility tree snapshots, and then interact with the page by simulating human user input.”9:1

Under the product names, almost every actuating agent runs the same loop.

  1. Observe. Capture the current state of the page: a screenshot, a serialised slice of the DOM, the accessibility tree, or some mix of the three.
  2. Decide. Send that observation, the user’s goal and the history so far to a model, and ask it for the next action.
  3. Act. Turn the model’s answer into a click at some coordinates, a keystroke, a scroll or a navigation.
  4. Repeat until the model decides the task is done, or gives up.

OpenAI’s description of its Computer-Using Agent is a good summary of how general this is. The model “processes raw pixel data to understand what’s happening on the screen and uses a virtual mouse and keyboard to complete actions.” Because it works through the graphical interface “just as humans do,” it can “perform digital tasks without using OS- or web-specific APIs.”11 Anthropic’s computer use documentation spells out the same loop from the developer’s side: the model asks for a screenshot or an action, your application performs it and returns the result, and the model asks again.12

That generality is actuation’s great strength. It needs nothing from the website. Any page a person can use, an agent can at least attempt to use, today, without anyone’s permission or cooperation. It is the reason browser agents could appear so quickly. It is also the source of almost everything that goes wrong with them.

Where actuation breaks

The explainer is blunt about the weakness. Many of the challenges assistive technology faces “also apply to AI agents that struggle to navigate existing human-first interfaces when agent-first ‘tools’ are not available,” and “even when agents succeed, simple operations often require multiple steps and can be slow or unreliable.”9:2 Lars’s tent shopping touched most of the failure modes. They fall into four groups.

Layout changes

An actuating agent infers what the site does from how the site looks. Every inference is tied to the presentation of a particular day. Rename “Add to cart” to “Add to bag”, move the filters from a sidebar to a drawer, swap a native <select> for a custom listbox, and the inference has to be made again. Sometimes the model makes it again correctly. Sometimes it doesn’t, and the failure is silent: the agent fills in the wrong field, or reports success when nothing happened.

The people who caused the breakage have no way of knowing. Trailhead’s designers ran their usability tests with people, not agents. Nothing in their tooling tells them that the redesign that improved human conversion just broke every assistant that used to shop there.

Ambiguous controls

Human interfaces lean on context that people supply without noticing. A field labelled “Name” might want a full name or only a first name. A date picker on a hotel site might be setting check-in or check-out depending on which half of the form you are in. A quantity stepper might add to the cart immediately, or only when you press the button below it. Chrome’s documentation gives the first example as a reason to build tools: a tool can tell an agent whether “a field requires a full name versus a separate first and last name.”7:2

People resolve this kind of ambiguity from experience. Agents resolve it by guessing, and the guesses are only as good as the model’s reading of a screenshot.

Multi-step forms and live state

Real tasks are rarely one click. Booking, checkout, filing a support ticket and changing a subscription are sequences of steps, each depending on state left by the last: a filtered result list, a selected time slot, an item in a cart, a half-completed form. Single-page applications change that state asynchronously, and much of it is invisible. An agent that reads the page too early sees stale results, as Lars’s agent did. An agent that reads it too late may have missed a toast message that has already faded. Each extra step is another observation, another model call and another chance to drift.

Hostile content

The fourth failure mode is newer, and it is the one that worries browser makers most. An actuating agent reads everything on the page as potential guidance, including text the site’s owner never wrote: a product review, a forum comment, an email in a webmail inbox. In August 2025, Brave’s security team showed how this could be exploited in Perplexity’s Comet. Instructions hidden behind a spoiler tag in a Reddit comment were enough to make the assistant, when a user asked it to summarise the page, open the user’s Perplexity account page to read their email address, trigger a one-time password, read it from their already signed-in Gmail, and post both back as a reply to the comment.13 Brave’s conclusion was that “traditional protections such as same-origin policy (SOP) or cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) are all effectively useless” when an agent follows instructions from untrusted content with the user’s full privileges.13:1

Anthropic published its own numbers the same month. In red-team testing of 123 prompt-injection test cases across 29 attack scenarios, browser use without its new mitigations showed “a 23.6% attack success rate”. The mitigations brought that down to 11.2 per cent, and a set of browser-specific attacks, such as form fields hidden in the DOM, went from 35.7 per cent to zero.1:2 Better, but not zero across the board, and the company was explicit that it wanted “to get these percentages much closer to zero” before a wide release.1:3

Prompt injection isn’t only a problem for actuation. Any agent that reads untrusted text has it, including agents that call tools, and Chapter 12 deals with it at length. But actuation makes it worse in a specific way: when everything on the page is input to the model, the page’s content and its controls are indistinguishable. A structured interface draws a line between the two.

The bill: cost, latency and reliability

Suppose actuation worked every time. It would still be expensive, because of the shape of the loop. Every step costs at least one model call, and every call carries an observation.

Observations are not small. Anthropic’s documentation for its computer use tool notes that long agent loops “accumulate screenshots quickly (roughly 1,000–1,800 input tokens each).”12:1 A task like Lars’s, at a few dozen steps, spends tens of thousands of input tokens on screenshots alone, and more if the agent keeps earlier screenshots in its history so the model can see what changed. DOM and accessibility-tree snapshots trade pixels for text but are often no smaller. None of that is the model reasoning about tents. It is the model working out where the buttons are.

Latency follows from the same arithmetic. Each step is a round trip to a model plus the time for the page to react. Anthropic lists latency first among the limitations of computer use: it “might be too slow compared to regular human-directed computer actions,” so developers should “focus on use cases where speed isn’t critical.”12:2 OpenAI, introducing agent mode in Atlas, called it “an early experience” that “may make mistakes on complex workflows,” and said it was improving “reliability, latency and complex task success.”4:1

Reliability is the hardest cost to see, because it shows up as a percentage on a benchmark rather than as a bill. WebArena, a benchmark built from fully functional websites in four common domains (e-commerce, social forums, collaborative software development and content management), gave the field its first sobering number in 2023: the best GPT-4-based agent of the time completed 14.41 per cent of tasks end to end, against 78.24 per cent for humans.14 Agents have improved fast since then. OpenAI later reported that its Computer-Using Agent reached 58.1 per cent on WebArena and 87 per cent on WebVoyager, a benchmark of simpler tasks on live websites, while noting that it “still needs more improvements to close the gap with human performance on more complex benchmarks like WebArena.”11:1 Those numbers will keep climbing, and you should check current figures rather than trust these. But the structure of the problem won’t change: an agent that has to rediscover the interface on every visit is always one misread away from failure, and the more steps a task takes, the more misreads it can accumulate.

Still in flux: agent benchmarks

Benchmark results for browser agents move every few months, and vendors report them on different task sets, step budgets and dates. The figures in this section are the ones published in the cited sources: WebArena’s original 2023 baselines and the results OpenAI published for its Computer-Using Agent. Treat them as illustrations of the gap, not as a current league table.

Figure 1.2 puts the two styles of interaction side by side. On the left is the loop described above. On the right is the alternative the rest of this book is about: the page tells the agent what it can do, as a named tool with a typed input, and the agent asks for it in one call.

Table 1.1 summarises the difference.

Actuation Structured tools
What the agent sees Pixels, DOM or accessibility tree Tool names, descriptions and input schemas
Model calls per task One or more per click, keystroke or scroll Roughly one per meaningful action
Effect of a redesign Can break silently None, as long as the tool contract holds
Ambiguity Resolved by the model’s guess Resolved by the site’s description and schema
Who decides the path The agent The site, with the agent choosing among offered tools
Needs site cooperation No Yes

Table 1.1 — Actuation and structured tools compared.

The last row matters. Structured interaction isn’t free: someone has to build the tools, and that someone is the site. That is why the next question is not “how do agents get better at clicking?” but “why would a website bother?”

Why sites have a stake

It is tempting to treat agent reliability as the agent maker’s problem. The agent is theirs, the model is theirs, the bill is theirs. But look at the tent purchase from Trailhead’s side.

The site loses the sale when the agent fails. If the agent gives up on a confusing filter sidebar, it doesn’t file a bug report. It tells the user it couldn’t do it, or it goes to a competitor whose site happened to be easier to operate. A site that agents can use reliably is, quite literally, a better shop for customers who send agents.

The site has no say in how it is used. An actuating agent decides for itself which path to take through your site. It may wander into the account settings to look for a delivery address, or fill in a form your support team would rather it didn’t. The explainer frames this as a matter of control. WebMCP will give agents “an alternative means to interact with the web that give the web developer more control over whether and how an AI-based agent interacts with their site.”9:3

The site risks being replaced by an integration. The obvious way to make an agent reliable is to skip the website and call an API. That works for some tasks, and Chapter 3 covers the Model Context Protocol, which makes it easy. But the explainer lists what it costs interactive web applications: the user interface is bypassed and context is lost, state and authentication have to be replicated on a separate server, and the site has to build and run that server.9:4 Its goal is the opposite, to “prevent disintermediation of web apps by backend integrations by adapting front-ends for use by agents, rather than replacing them.”15 For many businesses, the website is where the brand, the upsell and the relationship live. Chrome’s documentation makes the same point from the user’s side: tools that run visibly on the page mean “users gain trust that tasks are completed as expected,” and this “keeps your brand and human-centered design choices intact.”7:3

The site already has the code. Everything an agent needs to search Trailhead’s catalogue, add an item to a cart or read the cart back already exists in Trailhead’s front end, because the human interface needs it too. The explainer’s goal of code reuse says exactly this: “Any task that a user can accomplish through a page’s UI can be turned into a tool by reusing much of the page’s existing client-side code.”15:1

Put together, these points turn agent-readiness from a favour to agent vendors into ordinary product work. Like accessibility, search-engine optimisation or a good mobile layout, it is a way of making your product work for how people now arrive at it.

Humans and agents in the same tab

There is one more reason to care, and it shapes the whole of WebMCP: in the browser, the user is usually right there.

The agents in this chapter mostly work in the user’s own browser, in tabs the user can see, with the user’s signed-in sessions. That is a very different setting from an agent working on a server overnight. It allows a kind of cooperation that backend integrations struggle to offer: the agent does the tedious part, the user watches, corrects and approves.

Agent makers have built their safety stories around this. OpenAI’s Operator asked the user to take over when entering “sensitive information into the browser, such as login credentials or payment information,” and, before “finalizing any significant action, such as submitting an order or sending an email,” it “should ask for approval.”8:1 Claude in Chrome asks users “before taking high-risk actions like publishing, purchasing, or sharing personal data,” and lets them grant or revoke access per site.1:4 Google described its own goal for Gemini in Chrome as “you’ll remain in control as Chrome handles the tedious work.”3:1

What these safeguards have in common is that the agent decides when to ask. The site, which knows which of its actions are consequential, has no way to say so. Is “Add to cart” reversible? Is “Place order” the point of no return, or is there another confirmation screen? Is the footprint offer in the slide-in drawer an ad or part of the purchase? An actuating agent has to guess, and so does its safety layer.

The WebMCP explainer puts this cooperation first among its goals. The very first item is to “enable human-in-the-loop workflows,” supporting “cooperative scenarios where users delegate tasks to AI agents while maintaining visibility, history, and control over web pages.”15:2 Its non-goals are just as telling. WebMCP is not meant for “fully autonomous workflows” where no browser interface is present, and it is not a “replacement of human interfaces”: “The human web interface remains primary; agent tools augment rather than replace user interaction.”15:3 Chrome’s documentation lists the corresponding limitation candidly. While tools may work in headless environments, the API is “primarily designed for local browser workflows with a human in the loop.”7:4

This is the picture to carry through the book. The page stays the user’s page. The agent is a capable assistant sitting beside the user, and the site gives it proper tools instead of leaving it to poke at the buttons. When an action matters, the site can show its own confirmation, in its own interface, and the user clicks it. Fjord Table’s book_table tool does exactly this in Chapter 5.

Structured interaction, briefly

What would it take for Lars’s agent to do its job without guessing? Trailhead would need a way to tell the agent, in a form a model can use directly, what it offers: “I can search products by query, category, maximum price and stock status. I can compare two to four products. I can add a product to the cart. I can show you the cart.” Each capability would have a name, a plain-language description and a precise description of its inputs, and calling it would run Trailhead’s own code in Lars’s tab, updating the page he is looking at.

That is a tool, in the sense the AI industry has used the word since 2023. Chapter 2 explains how tools became the common unit of agent capability, from function calling in model APIs to OpenAPI-based plug-ins and agent protocols. Chapter 3 covers the Model Context Protocol, which standardised tools for backend services. Chapter 4 introduces WebMCP, which brings the same idea into the page. Its specification describes the result in one sentence: pages that use WebMCP “can be thought of as Model Context Protocol servers that implement tools in client-side script instead of on the backend.”2:2

WebMCP is not finished, and it is not uncontroversial. Chapter 4 and Chapter 15 cover the politics in detail. For now, two facts are enough. Chrome and Edge are both running origin trials of the API, so you can ship it to real users in those browsers today, and Chrome also offers a flag for local development.167:5 And Chrome’s documentation positions it the way this book does: WebMCP “offers higher accuracy for agentic task completion, and it can be added as a progressive enhancement.”7:6 Your site keeps working exactly as before for people and for actuating agents. Agents that understand tools get a better way in.

Still in flux: the agent landscape

The products named in this chapter change quickly. Assistants gain and lose agent features, extensions move out of preview, and pricing and availability vary by country. WebMCP support among agents is younger still. As of 15 October 2026, the explainer’s implementation status page lists ChatGPT Desktop as supporting WebMCP, experimental support in Brave’s Leo, and Meta Ray-Ban Display as “coming soon”.16:1 Check that page, rather than this chapter, before you decide which agents your tools will meet first.

The projects in this book

Concepts are easier to hold on to when they are attached to something you are building. Four projects run through the book. You will meet them properly in the chapters that use them, but here is the cast, with the chapters where each one does most of its work (Table 1.2 and Figure 1.3).

Fjord Table is a small restaurant in Oslo with a booking page. It is deliberately modest: a date, a time, a party size and a seating preference. It is the book’s first WebMCP site. Chapter 4 uses it to show the idea, and Chapter 5 gives it two tools, search_availability and book_table, the second of which never completes a booking without the guest confirming it in Fjord Table’s own dialog. Chapter 8 rebuilds its form with the experimental declarative API, Chapter 9 takes it end to end, from flag to deployment, and Chapter 14 puts its tools under test.

Trailhead is the outdoor-gear store from this chapter’s opening: a React and TypeScript storefront with prices in Norwegian kroner. It is the book’s main production-shaped app. Its tools are search_products, compare_products, add_to_cart, get_cart and checkout, and the last one is marked as consequential, so the page shows its own confirmation and nothing is bought without the user’s click. Trailhead also gets a companion backend MCP server in Chapter 3, which makes the difference between server-side and in-page tools concrete. It carries the chapters on annotations and errors, frameworks, tool design, security, privacy, testing and the business case.

Helpdesk Widget is a support widget made by a fictional vendor, Supportly, and embedded in a fictional accounting dashboard, Ledgerly. The widget and the dashboard come from different origins, which is exactly the situation where the web’s security model gets interesting. Its tools (search_articles, create_ticket and get_ticket_status) are the book’s test case for cross-origin rules and page-embedded agents in Chapter 7, and for the threat models in Chapter 12.

Test Agent is optional. It is a minimal agent harness, built either as an extension or as an in-page agent using Chrome’s on-device model through the Prompt API, which you can use to call your tools and run evaluations without depending on any particular commercial assistant. It is built in Chapter 9, and Chapter 14 runs it as the in-page counterpart to its eval harness.

Every code listing in the book is also in the companion repository, webmaxru/webmcp-book-demos on GitHub, organised by chapter, with tests that run each example against a mock of the API and, where possible, against Chromium with WebMCP enabled.17 This chapter and the next have no code. From Chapter 3 on, almost every chapter does.

What this book will and will not cover

This is a book for people who build web applications and want to make them work well with AI agents. It assumes you are comfortable with JavaScript, and for some chapters with TypeScript and React. It does not assume you know anything about AI agents, MCP or WebMCP.

Here is what it covers.

  • Why. Part I (Chapters 1 to 4) explains the problem, the history of tools as the unit of agent capability, the Model Context Protocol, and where WebMCP came from.
  • The API. Part II (Chapters 5 to 8) covers WebMCP in depth: registering tools, annotations, the life of a tool call, errors and cancellation, frames and origins, and the declarative form-based API that Chrome still ships but the specification has dropped.
  • Building. Part III (Chapters 9 to 11) builds real apps: a first app end to end, WebMCP in React and Angular, and how to design tools that agents actually use well.
  • Trust. Part IV (Chapters 12 and 13) covers threat models, prompt injection, privacy, consent and keeping the human in the loop.
  • Shipping. Part V (Chapters 14 and 15) covers testing, debugging and evaluations, and an honest map of browser support and the standards process.
  • Strategy. Part VI (Chapters 16 and 17) is for product managers and technical leaders as much as for developers: what agent-readiness means for a business, and where things are heading.

If you are a product manager or a tech lead, you can read Part I, the opening of each chapter, Part IV’s discussion of risk, and Part VI without following the code.

Here is what it does not cover.

  • How to build an agent. The book is about the site’s side of the conversation. It explains enough about agents to make sense of how your tools will be used, and the optional Test Agent is deliberately small. It is not a guide to prompting, model selection or agent frameworks.
  • Backend integrations in depth. Chapter 3 teaches enough MCP to build a working server and to understand WebMCP’s vocabulary. For production MCP servers, the protocol’s own documentation goes much further.
  • Making actuation better. Your site should still work well for agents that click, and much of what makes a site easier for agents to click through (semantic HTML, proper labels, a good accessibility tree) is also good for people. The explainer is explicit that WebMCP “will not conflict with these existing automation techniques.”9:5 But this book is about the structured alternative, not about tuning your markup for screenshot readers.
  • A stable standard. There isn’t one yet. WebMCP is a draft. The current version of the specification, dated 15 October 2026, describes itself as a Draft Community Group Report that “is not a W3C Standard nor is it on the W3C Standards Track.”2:3 The book teaches the API as it stands in that draft and in the Chromium origin trials, flags every part that is unsettled with a Still in flux box like the ones in this chapter, and explains the debates so that you can follow them after publication.

Still in flux: reading a book about a moving target

Every factual claim about the specification, browsers and vendors in this book carries a footnote to a source, with the date it was checked. Most were checked in mid-October 2026. When a footnote and the live specification disagree, the specification wins. Appendix D collects the API changes that have already happened, so you can recognise older code when you see it.

Chapter summary

  • Browser agents are agents that act on web pages on a user’s behalf. They come built into browsers (Gemini in Chrome, Perplexity’s Comet, and for a while OpenAI’s ChatGPT Atlas), as extensions (Claude in Chrome), and embedded in pages, sometimes running an on-device model.
  • Today most of them work by actuation: observing the page through screenshots, DOM and accessibility-tree snapshots, then simulating clicks and keystrokes, one model call per step.
  • Actuation needs nothing from the site, which is why it spread so fast. It also breaks on layout changes, ambiguous controls and multi-step flows, and it treats everything on the page, including hostile text, as potential instructions.
  • It is expensive and slow. Each screenshot costs roughly a thousand or more input tokens, vendors list latency as a known limitation, and published benchmarks still show a gap between agents and people on complex web tasks.
  • Sites have a stake: they lose sales when agents fail, have no say in how agents use them, risk being bypassed by backend integrations, and already have the front-end code that agents need.
  • In the browser the user is usually present. WebMCP’s first goal is human-in-the-loop cooperation, not full autonomy, and it lets the site, which knows which of its actions matter, show its own confirmations.
  • The alternative is structured interaction: the page offers named, described, schema-typed tools, and the agent calls them. Chapter 2 traces how tools became the industry’s unit of agent capability. Chapter 3 covers MCP, and Chapter 4 introduces WebMCP.
  • Four projects run through the book: Fjord Table, Trailhead, Helpdesk Widget and the optional Test Agent. Their code lives in the companion repository.

Part I · Why the web needs an agent interface

Chapter 2: From APIs to Tools: A Short History

“Every new data source requires its own custom implementation, making truly connected systems difficult to scale.”

— Anthropic, “Introducing the Model Context Protocol”1

One capability, many descriptions

Trailhead, the outdoor-gear store from Chapter 1, has one capability that every agent wants: product search. Give it a query, an optional category, a maximum price in kroner and an “in stock only” flag, and it returns a list of products. Trailhead’s own React front end calls it dozens of times an hour.

Now imagine the requests arriving at Trailhead’s engineering team over a few years. In 2023, someone asks for a ChatGPT plug-in, which means an OpenAPI description and a manifest file. Later that year, the plug-in becomes a GPT action. The mobile team wants their in-app assistant to call search through OpenAI’s function calling, then a second assistant uses Anthropic’s API, which describes the same function with a slightly different envelope. In 2025, someone asks for an MCP server so that desktop assistants can find Trailhead’s products. A partner wants Trailhead’s “gear advisor” agent to be discoverable by other companies’ agents over A2A. And in 2026, the product team asks why the browser’s built-in assistant still clicks through the filter sidebar instead of just searching.

Each request is reasonable. Each one describes the same capability, a name, a sentence about what it does and a schema for its inputs, in a slightly different place. That repetition is the story of this chapter. It explains how the tool (a named, described, schema-typed capability that a model can choose to call) became the common unit of agent capability, why the industry kept reinventing the envelope around it, and why the browser tab was the last major place left without one.

The chapter has no code, but it introduces the vocabulary the rest of the book relies on. If you have built with function calling or MCP before, you can skim it. If you haven’t, it is the shortest path to understanding why WebMCP looks the way it does.

Before tools: APIs for programs

Long before anyone asked a language model to book a table, the web had a well-developed way for one program to use another: the web API. Roy Fielding’s 2000 doctoral dissertation gave the dominant style its name, Representational State Transfer (REST), and the idea of resources addressed by URLs and manipulated with a small set of HTTP methods.2 By the 2010s almost every serious web product had an HTTP API alongside its user interface.

APIs designed for programs come with an assumption that matters later in this story: the caller is a developer who reads the documentation once, writes code against it, and then runs that code many times. The documentation can be long and the conventions can be subtle, because a human reads it and a compiler enforces the result.

That assumption pushed the industry towards machine-readable API descriptions, so that client code, documentation and tests could be generated rather than written by hand. The one that won is the OpenAPI Specification. It began as the Swagger Specification, which SmartBear Software donated to what became the OpenAPI Initiative, an open governance project under the Linux Foundation.3 An OpenAPI document lists an API’s operations, their parameters, request bodies and responses. The latest published version at the time of writing is 3.2.1, dated 10 September 2026.4

Inside OpenAPI documents, the shapes of request and response bodies are described with JSON Schema, a vocabulary for saying what a JSON value must look like: its type, its properties, which ones are required, which strings are allowed. JSON Schema has its own specification, and its current version is called 2020-12.5 Remember that name. JSON Schema is the thread that runs through every stage of this chapter, and WebMCP’s inputSchema is a JSON Schema too.

By the early 2020s, then, the web already had a common language for describing capabilities to programs. What it didn’t have was a caller that could read a description and decide, on its own, when to use it.

Teaching models to use tools

Large language models changed who the caller could be. In October 2022, the ReAct paper showed that a model could interleave “reasoning traces and task-specific actions”, so that the actions let it “interface with external sources” and the reasoning helped it plan and handle exceptions.6 In February 2023, the Toolformer paper showed that a model could “teach themselves to use external tools via simple APIs”, deciding “which APIs to call, when to call them, what arguments to pass, and how to best incorporate the results”.7

Those two sentences describe the loop that every agent in this book runs. The model gets a goal and a list of things it can do. It decides whether to do one of them, and with what arguments. Something outside the model performs the action and hands back the result. The model reads the result and decides what to do next.

Research prototypes taught models to emit tool calls in ad hoc text formats that the surrounding program had to parse. That worked in papers. It didn’t work well enough for products, because a model that is almost right about the format produces a call that a parser rejects, or worse, one that it accepts with the wrong arguments. What products needed was a contract: a way for the developer to declare the available tools, and for the model to answer with a call that matched the declaration.

Function calling: JSON Schema becomes the lingua franca

That contract arrived in model APIs in 2023. In June of that year, OpenAI announced that developers could “describe functions” to two new model versions and “have the model intelligently choose to output a JSON object containing arguments to call those functions.”8 The models had been “fine-tuned to both detect when a function needs to be called (depending on the user’s input) and to respond with JSON that adheres to the function signature,” and developers described the functions “via JSON Schema”.8:1 OpenAI’s examples are a good summary of what tools are for. A request like “Email Anya to see if she wants to get coffee next Friday” becomes a call to send_email(to: string, body: string), and “Who are my top ten customers this month?” becomes an internal API call.8:2

The idea spread across the industry because it was simple and because JSON Schema was already familiar. Anthropic’s API defines a tool with a name, a description and an input_schema, and Claude answers with a tool_use block that your code executes.9 Google’s Gemini API offers function calling too, with schemas written in “a subset of the OpenAPI schema”.10 The field names differ slightly from one vendor to the next. The substance is the same everywhere: a name, a natural-language description, and a JSON Schema for the arguments.

Reliability came next. A model that produces JSON “that adheres to the function signature” most of the time still produces broken calls some of the time. In August 2024, OpenAI introduced Structured Outputs, which constrains generation so that outputs “reliably adhere to developer-supplied JSON Schemas.” For function calling it is enabled “by setting strict: true within your function definition,” and on OpenAI’s own evaluation of complex schema following, the new model scored 100 per cent against less than 40 per cent for the June 2023 model.11 The schema had become more than documentation for the model. It was a hard constraint on its output.

The round trip, step by step

It is worth slowing down to see what actually happens in a function call, because WebMCP keeps the same shape. Take Trailhead’s mobile assistant, built on a model API with function calling, and a customer who types “any two-person tents under 4,000 kroner in stock?”

  1. The application declares its tools. Along with the conversation, it sends the model a list of tool definitions. One of them is search_products, with a description (“Search Trailhead’s catalogue by keyword, category, maximum price in NOK and stock status”) and a JSON Schema saying that query is a required string, category is one of five values, maxPrice is a number and inStockOnly is a boolean.
  2. The model decides. It reads the request and the tool descriptions and concludes that this question needs a search. Instead of answering in prose, it returns a structured call: the tool’s name and a JSON object of arguments, query set to “two-person tent”, category to “tents”, maxPrice to 4000 and inStockOnly to true.
  3. The application acts. The app’s code, not the model, checks the arguments, calls Trailhead’s search API with them, and gets back a list of products.
  4. The result goes back to the model. The app sends the products to the model as the result of that call.
  5. The model answers, or calls again. It might summarise three tents for the customer, or call a second tool to compare two of them.

Notice what the model never does: it never touches Trailhead’s systems directly. It only proposes calls. Everything that has an effect happens in code the developer controls, which is also where checks, logging and confirmations go. Notice, too, that the model’s choice depends almost entirely on two pieces of text, the tool’s name and its description, plus the schema. Those three things are the whole interface between the model and the capability.

Three properties of function calling carry straight through to WebMCP, and it is worth naming them now.

  • The description is written for a model. It is not API reference documentation for a developer. It has to tell a model, in a sentence or two, when this tool is the right choice and when it isn’t. Chapter 11 is about writing these well.
  • The schema is the contract. It tells the model what arguments are valid, and it gives the receiving code a way to check them. In WebMCP, as Chapter 5 shows, the browser passes the schema to the agent but does not validate calls against it, so your code still has to.
  • The model chooses, and your code acts. Function calling never executes anything by itself. The model proposes a call; the application decides whether and how to run it. That separation is what makes it possible to put a human confirmation step in the middle, which WebMCP relies on.

Function calling solved the problem of expressing a tool call. It didn’t solve the problem of distributing tools. In the original design, the developer of each application wrote the tool definitions into their own code. If Trailhead wanted its search to be usable by someone else’s assistant, it needed a way to publish the definition and have that assistant pick it up.

OpenAPI meets the chatbot: plug-ins and actions

The first big attempt to solve distribution came before function calling was even public in the API. On 23 March 2023, OpenAI announced “experimental support for AI plugins in ChatGPT — tools designed specifically for language models.”12 The design reused the web’s existing description format. To build a plug-in, a developer would “build an API with endpoints you’d like a language model to call,” then “create an OpenAPI specification documenting your API, and a manifest file that links to the OpenAPI spec and includes some plugin-specific metadata.”13 The manifest carried fields such as name_for_model and description_for_model, separate from the names and descriptions shown to people, and when a user enabled a plug-in, its documentation was “shown to the language model as part of the conversation.”13:1 OpenTable, Instacart, Wolfram and Zapier were among the launch partners.13:2

This was a significant moment for anyone who builds websites, for two reasons. It confirmed that an existing, widely used API description format could be repurposed as a tool description with very little extra work. And it showed the separation of audiences that WebMCP later formalises: a name and description for the model, and a different presentation for the human.

The plug-in beta did not last in that form. In November 2023, OpenAI introduced GPTs, custom versions of ChatGPT, and with them actions: developers “can also define custom actions by making one or more APIs available to the GPT. Like plugins, actions allow GPTs to integrate external data or interact with the real-world.”1412:1 The envelope changed; the idea of an API described for a model stayed.

Still in flux: the word “plugin”

Product names in this space are recycled freely. In 2026 the word “plugin” is back in ChatGPT, now for packages that bundle skills, connected apps and interactive extensions, and OpenAI’s release notes describe supported plugins using MCP events to trigger automations.1512:2 These have little in common with the 2023 plug-ins beyond the name. When you read about “plugins”, “actions”, “apps” or “connectors”, check the date and the vendor before assuming you know what is meant.

Plug-ins and actions had one more property that matters for the next section: they were specific to one platform. An OpenAPI document was portable, but the manifest, the review process, the authentication flow and the user experience belonged to ChatGPT. A company that wanted to reach users of several assistants had to repeat the exercise for each of them.

The description is the new documentation

Plug-ins made one lesson explicit that function calling had left implicit. An API has two audiences now. The manifest’s name_for_human and description_for_human were for the person browsing a plug-in store; name_for_model and description_for_model were for the model deciding whether to call it.13:3 Those are different jobs, and they need different writing.

Documentation for developers can be long, because developers read it once and then write code. A tool description is read by a model every time it decides what to do, often alongside dozens of other descriptions, and it has a sentence or two to say when this tool is the right one. It is closer to a prompt than to reference documentation. Get it wrong and the model calls the tool when it shouldn’t, doesn’t call it when it should, or fills in the arguments badly. No compiler will tell you.

The same advice has turned up in every generation of the technology, and Chrome’s WebMCP guidance states the current version of it clearly. “A clear description should describe what the tool does and when to use it,” it says, and it recommends positive language over prohibitions: rather than “Don’t use this tool for weather,” write “This tool can create a calendar event, scheduled for a specific date and time.”16 It also warns against names that hide what a tool does, contrasting a create-event tool that creates an event immediately with a start-event-creation-process tool that only redirects the user to a form.16:1

The point for this chapter is that the description travelled with the tool through every envelope. Function definitions, plug-in manifests, GPT actions, MCP tools and WebMCP tools all carry one, and in each of them it does the same job. A team that learns to write good tool descriptions for one of these formats has learned it for all of them. Chapter 11 is devoted to doing it well for WebMCP.

Why one integration per platform doesn’t scale

Step back from the vendor names and look at the arithmetic. Suppose there are N AI applications that want to use tools, and M services that want to offer them. If every pairing needs its own integration, someone has to build and maintain up to N × M of them. Ten assistants and a thousand services is ten thousand integrations, each with its own manifest format, authentication flow, review process and quirks. Most will never be built. The ones that are will drift out of date.

A shared protocol changes the sum. If every assistant speaks the protocol as a client, and every service speaks it as a server, the work is N + M: each side implements the protocol once. Figure 2.1 shows the difference. This is the same argument that made HTTP, USB and the Language Server Protocol worth standardising, and it is the argument Anthropic made when it open-sourced the Model Context Protocol on 25 November 2024. “Every new data source requires its own custom implementation,” the announcement said, “making truly connected systems difficult to scale.” MCP was offered as “a universal, open standard for connecting AI systems with data sources, replacing fragmented integrations with a single protocol.”1:1

Chapter 3 covers MCP in depth, so here are only the facts this chapter needs. MCP defines hosts (the AI applications), clients (connectors inside a host) and servers (the services that offer capabilities), and they communicate with JSON-RPC 2.0 messages.17 Among the things a server can offer are tools, and an MCP tool definition will look very familiar by now: a name, an optional title, a description and an inputSchema, which is a JSON Schema.18 The current version of the protocol is dated 2026-07-28.17:1

What changed with MCP was not the shape of a tool. It was who owned the envelope. Function definitions belonged to whoever wrote the application. Plug-in manifests belonged to one platform. MCP belonged to nobody in particular, and on 9 December 2025 Anthropic made that formal by donating it to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation “co-founded by Anthropic, Block and OpenAI, with support from Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Cloudflare, and Bloomberg.”19 The foundation launched with three founding projects: MCP, Block’s goose and OpenAI’s AGENTS.md.20

For Trailhead, MCP collapses most of the list of requests at the start of this chapter into one: build an MCP server once, and every assistant that speaks MCP can search the catalogue. Chapter 3 builds exactly that server.

Agents talking to agents

Tools assume a particular relationship: an agent in charge, calling capabilities that do what they are told and return a result. Not every interaction fits. Sometimes the thing on the other end is itself an agent, with its own model, its own judgment and its own long-running work. A travel agent might hand a hotel search to a hotel chain’s booking agent and wait for it to negotiate dates; Trailhead’s gear advisor might be asked by a hiking app’s agent to recommend a tent and come back an hour later when stock arrives.

On 9 April 2025, Google announced the Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) for this case, “with support and contributions from more than 50 technology partners.”21 Google described it as “an open protocol that complements Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP), which provides helpful tools and context to agents.”21:1 Its specification describes A2A as “an open standard designed to facilitate communication and interoperability between independent, potentially opaque AI agent systems.”22 Opaque is the key word. Where an MCP server exposes individual tools with schemas, an A2A agent exposes itself: it publishes an Agent Card, a JSON document describing what it can do and how to reach it, which other agents can fetch from a well-known location such as /.well-known/agent-card.json.22:121:2 The calling agent delegates a task; the remote agent decides how to carry it out.

A2A followed the same path to neutral governance as MCP, only faster. The Linux Foundation launched the A2A project on 23 June 2025.23 The specification reached version 1.0.0.22:2 And in August 2026, A2A was accepted as a Growth Stage project at the same Agentic AI Foundation that hosts MCP.24 The announcement described the division of labour neatly: MCP “serves as the vertical integration layer connecting agents to internal tools and databases,” while A2A “acts as the horizontal protocol enabling peer-to-peer collaboration.”24:1

A2A is not the only proposal for agents talking to agents, and this book doesn’t go further into the category. It matters here for what it shares with everything else in this chapter. A2A connects agents running on servers, over the network, each authenticated in its own way. Like MCP servers, OpenAPI plug-ins and function calls, it assumes the capability lives somewhere an agent can reach without a user’s browser.

Still in flux: protocol governance

Both MCP and A2A now sit under the Agentic AI Foundation, and both continue to version their specifications: MCP by date (the current version is 2026-07-28) and A2A by number (1.0.0 at the time of writing).17:222:3 Membership, project stages and the relationship between the two protocols are likely to keep changing. Check the foundation’s and the projects’ own pages for the current picture.

Where the browser fits

Put the whole history on one line, as in Figure 2.2, and a pattern appears. Every stage moved tools further from any particular application and closer to a shared, neutral description. Every stage also kept tools on the server side.

That server-side bias is not an accident. It follows from who the callers were: model APIs running in data centres, chat assistants running in the cloud, agents talking to agents over the network. For those callers, the natural place for a capability is an HTTP endpoint.

But Chapter 1 showed where a growing share of agent work actually happens: in the user’s browser, in a tab where the user is already signed in, looking at a page that already holds the state they care about. For that kind of work, every integration in this chapter has the same three weaknesses. The WebMCP explainer groups MCP and OpenAPI together as backend integrations and lists them.25

  • The interface is bypassed. The agent talks to the service’s backend, and the page the user is looking at doesn’t change. Trailhead’s cart, filled through an MCP server, doesn’t update the cart badge in the tab the user has open until something reloads it.
  • State and authentication have to be duplicated. The user is signed in to the tab. The backend integration needs its own credentials and its own idea of what the user is doing.
  • There is a second thing to build. Trailhead’s front end already knows how to search, filter and add to the cart. A backend integration means writing and operating a separate server to do the same things.

Chrome’s documentation puts the contrast in one sentence. WebMCP “accesses live session data, cookies, and DOM elements that are available only in a live browser tab. Instead of your application being a guest within an agent, the agent is a guest on your platform.”26

That is the gap WebMCP fills. It keeps everything this chapter built up (a tool with a name, a description written for a model, a JSON Schema for its inputs, a model that chooses and code that acts) and moves the code into the page. The WebMCP explainer describes pages that use it as “in-page Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that implement tools exposing client-side logic and DOM interaction rather than server-side APIs.”25:1 The explainer’s repository was created on 5 August 2025, a little over eight months after MCP’s launch.27

Why not just run MCP in the browser?

If WebMCP is “in-page MCP”, why not simply put an MCP server in the page and let the browser’s agent connect to it as an MCP client? The WebMCP explainer considered exactly that and gives two reasons for not doing it.28 First, “MCP was built primarily for server-to-client and stdio/SSE process communication. It lacks native web concepts like origins, standard browser permissions, DOM integration, and tab-level lifecycle management.” Second, “coupling a web API directly to an actively evolving backend protocol would hinder backward compatibility and platform stability.”28:1 Web APIs, once shipped, are very hard to change; MCP has published several dated versions and is still evolving.

So WebMCP takes MCP’s vocabulary and leaves its protocol behind. In the explainer’s words, it “shares a common vocabulary with MCP (e.g., tools, schemas, parameters), but provides a form-fitting, client-safe solution designed natively for the web platform.”28:2 The explainer’s list of prior art reads like a summary of this chapter: MCP; the community MCP-B project, which built “browser tab and extension transports for local in-page communication”; OpenAPI, “used in platform-specific extensions like ChatGPT Actions”; and A2A, “focused on connecting distinct autonomous AI agents to one another.”28:3

Chapter 4 tells the rest of that story, including the other alternatives the editors rejected. For now, the important point is the continuity. A developer who has written a function definition or an MCP tool will find a WebMCP tool immediately familiar: the same name, the same kind of description, the same JSON Schema. What is new is where the execute function runs and what it can reach.

Five approaches side by side

Table 2.1 lines up the approaches.

Function calling OpenAPI plug-ins and actions MCP A2A WebMCP
What is described Functions in your own app An HTTP API Tools, resources and prompts on a server A whole agent, via its Agent Card Tools in a web page
Who owns the envelope Each model vendor One assistant platform An open protocol (AAIF) An open protocol (AAIF) A W3C Community Group draft
Where the code runs Your application Your backend Your server or local process The remote agent The user’s tab
Uses the user’s live session Only if your app does No No No Yes
Typical caller Your own app’s model One assistant Any MCP host Another agent A browser agent
Schema language JSON Schema (vendor subsets) OpenAPI / JSON Schema JSON Schema Agent Card (JSON) JSON Schema

Table 2.1 — Five ways to give an agent a capability. All but A2A describe tools with a name, a description and a JSON Schema; they differ in who owns the format and where the code runs.

None of these replaces the others. A store like Trailhead might reasonably use all five: function calling inside its own support chatbot, an MCP server for desktop assistants and back-office agents, an A2A agent card for its gear advisor, and WebMCP tools on its storefront for the browser agents its customers already use. The rest of the book is about the last one, but it borrows freely from the others. The vocabulary of tools comes from function calling, the shape of a tool definition comes from MCP, and the hard-won lessons about descriptions, schemas and confirmation steps apply everywhere.

What the history teaches

Three lessons from this short history shape the rest of the book.

The core of a tool is stable; the envelope is not. A name, a description for a model and a JSON Schema for the inputs have survived every generation since 2023, while the formats wrapped around them (functions, plug-in manifests, actions, MCP tool lists) came and went. The practical consequence is that time spent designing good tools is never wasted. If WebMCP changes shape again before it settles, and Chapter 4 explains why it might, your names, descriptions and schemas will move to the new shape with little change.

Distribution is the hard part. Expressing a tool call turned out to be easy once JSON Schema was in place. Getting the right tools in front of the right agent, with the right authentication, without building an integration per platform, is what took years and several false starts. WebMCP’s answer to distribution is unusual: the tools are discovered by visiting the page, so the page itself is the distribution channel. That has real limits, which Chrome lists honestly (“Clients and browsers must visit a site directly to know if it has callable tools”), and real advantages, which Part III explores.29

Someone has to own the decision to act. From function calling onward, the model proposes and code disposes. The question each generation had to answer was whose code, and who gets asked before something irreversible happens. For server-side integrations, the answer is usually the assistant platform. For WebMCP, it is the site, in its own interface, with the user watching. That shift is the subject of Part IV.

Chapter summary

  • Web APIs, described with OpenAPI and JSON Schema, gave programs a common way to use services long before language models arrived. OpenAPI began as Swagger and is now governed under the Linux Foundation; JSON Schema’s current version is 2020-12.
  • Research such as ReAct (2022) and Toolformer (2023) showed that models could decide when to call tools and with what arguments. Products needed a stricter contract than free-text formats.
  • Function calling, introduced by OpenAI in June 2023 and adopted across vendors, made the tool a first-class concept: a name, a description written for a model, and a JSON Schema for the arguments. Structured Outputs (August 2024) turned the schema into a hard constraint.
  • ChatGPT plug-ins (March 2023) and then GPT actions (November 2023) used OpenAPI to distribute tools to an assistant, but each such integration belonged to one platform.
  • One integration per pairing means N × M connectors. MCP, open-sourced by Anthropic in November 2024 and donated to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025, reduces that to N + M. Its tools have a name, a description and an inputSchema.
  • A2A, announced by Google in April 2025 and now also under the Agentic AI Foundation, connects opaque agents to each other through Agent Cards rather than exposing individual tools.
  • Every one of these integrations runs on the server side, which bypasses the page, duplicates state and authentication, and means building a second system. WebMCP keeps the tool and moves it into the user’s tab. Chapter 3 now covers MCP properly, because WebMCP borrows its vocabulary.
