Part V · Shipping and the ecosystem

Chapter 15: Browser Support and the Standards Road

“Please note that Community Groups do not create W3C standards.”

— W3C, Community and Business Groups FAQ1

Two answers to one question

Suppose the Trailhead team asks the question every web team asks before adopting a new API: which browsers support it? There are two honest answers, and they are not the same.

The engineering answer fits in a sentence. Chromium-based browsers run WebMCP behind origin trials, so Chrome and Edge will expose document.modelContext on any page that carries a valid trial token. Every other engine doesn’t expose it at all. Chapter 5 showed the feature check that covers this, and this chapter extends it into a small module that tells you exactly which surface you are standing on.

The standards answer takes the rest of the chapter. WebMCP is a Community Group draft whose editors come from Microsoft and Google.2 Mozilla recorded a neutral position and Apple’s WebKit team an opposed one.34 The W3C Technical Architecture Group (TAG) has been reviewing it since June and has labelled it “Missing: Multi-stakeholder support”.5 An attempt to move the specification into an existing W3C Working Group ran into a threatened formal objection over the summer and was closed on 13 October. Its replacement, a new Agentic Web Working Group, is a draft charter in review as this chapter is written.67

Chapter 4 sketched this landscape in one table and promised to come back to it. This chapter does so in depth. It explains how to read each signal (a spec’s status line, a chromestatus entry, an origin trial page, a standards-position label, a TAG review), what each party has actually said, which agents and libraries consume WebMCP today, and what the possible routes from Community Group to standard would mean for a team that ships tools now. It closes with a script that re-checks all of it for you, because every fact in the following pages has a date on it.

Everything here was checked on 15 October 2026.

Reading the signals

Web standards news arrives through a handful of documents, each with its own vocabulary. Before going vendor by vendor, it helps to know what each one can and cannot tell you.

The specification’s status line. The top of the WebMCP draft reads “Draft Community Group Report, 15 October 2026”, and its status section says plainly that it “is not a W3C Standard nor is it on the W3C Standards Track.”2:1 The date changes whenever the editors publish, which during 2026 has meant every few days. A Community Group is an open forum anyone can join for free, and the W3C’s own FAQ asks members not to call its output “standards work” or “draft standards”. CG reports exist to make a later move to a Working Group easier: the contributor licence agreement is designed so that patent commitments carry over.1:1

The commit history. The status line tells you that the draft changed; the repository tells you what changed. For WebMCP, the history of webmachinelearning/webmcp is the most precise record there is of when an API was renamed, added or removed, and it is the source for every date in Table 15.1.8

chromestatus. Each Chromium feature has an entry listing its owners, the blink-dev “intent” threads, and its trial stages with milestone numbers. It also has a “browser signals” block for other engines and a standards-maturity field.9 Read the stages and milestones as authoritative, since Chromium engineers maintain them. Read the signals block with care: on 15 October 2026 it still said “No signal” for both Firefox and Safari, months after both had published positions. The entry was last edited on 28 September.9:1 The lesson generalises: a status page is only as current as its last edit, so go to the primary record whenever one exists.

Origin trial pages. Chrome and Edge each have a registration page per trial, with the trial’s description, its expiry and its terms.1011

Standards positions. Mozilla and WebKit both run public GitHub repositories where anyone can ask for an engine’s view of a proposal. The outcome is a label: position: neutral, position: oppose and so on. The discussion in the issue is where the reasons live.3:14:1

TAG design reviews. The TAG reviews proposals for architectural fit. Its labels track progress (“Progress: in progress”), the review type and the focus areas still pending, and, sometimes, a missing prerequisite.5:1

Figure 15.1 puts the main events from all of these sources on one timeline.

Chrome and Edge: two origin trials

Timelines

WebMCP reached Chromium in stages. chromestatus records a developer trial (the API behind a flag, for local testing) starting in Chrome 146, followed by an origin trial running from Chrome 149 through Chrome 156.9:2 Google announced the trial on 9 June 2026 with the words “In Chrome 149, you can sign up for the WebMCP origin trial.”12 On 28 September 2026 the trial gained an extension through Chrome 162. The reason chromestatus gives is unusually candid: “OT feedback has suggested improvements to the API, which we are implementing. The OT extension would enable us to get data on those improvements as well as to continue getting data on the rest of the feature.”9:3

Microsoft runs its own trial. The project’s implementation-status page says it is live in Edge 150, and the Edge registration page gives a trial expiration date of 30 March 2027.1311:1 Note that the two trials are measured differently: Chrome counts in milestones and Edge in calendar dates.

For local development no token is needed. Chrome’s documentation tells you to enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and relaunch; that flag corresponds to the WebMCPTesting feature this book’s demos pass to Chromium on the command line.14

Tokens

An origin trial lets a site use an experimental feature on its own origin, for real users, without those users touching any flags. You register your origin, receive a token, and serve that token with every page that should get the feature. Chrome’s origin-trial documentation lists three ways to deliver it: a <meta http-equiv="origin-trial"> tag in the <head>, an Origin-Trial HTTP response header, or a meta tag injected from script.10:1 Edge’s trial page offers the same meta-tag and header options, and its registration is separate from Chrome’s.11:2

The header form of the same thing, for a server or CDN configuration:

Origin-Trial: CHROME_TRIAL_TOKEN
Origin-Trial: EDGE_TRIAL_TOKEN

A page can carry several tokens, and Chrome ignores tokens that are invalid or expired.10:2 That makes Listing 15.1 safe to serve to every browser: each one picks out the token it recognises.

Three details of the token model matter in practice.

  • Third-party tokens. Both trials accept them: chromestatus records third-party support for the Chrome trial, and the Edge trial record has supportsThirdParty set to true.9:411:3 A third-party token lets a provider of embedded content, such as Supportly’s Helpdesk Widget from Chapter 7, enable the feature in its own script across every customer site. Chrome’s documentation adds a caution: a third-party token works only when injected by an external script, not in a meta tag, inline script or header.10:3
  • Extensions mean renewal. When a trial is extended, Chrome emails registrants, and each origin has to renew and deploy a new token.10:4 Anyone who shipped a Chrome 149 token and expects it to work through Chrome 162 should check the registration console now.
  • Measurement. The trial measures adoption with a Chromium use counter named kModelContextRegisterTool.9:5 Google’s stated goal for the experiment is “understanding the API ergonomics for agentic workflows across various verticals such as web commerce and productivity”, along with “metrics for tool usage and latency.”9:6

What can change during a trial

Origin trials exist to change an API. Chrome’s announcement calls trials “time-limited programs that offer early access to experimental platform features” whose goal is “informing future iterations of the API.”12:1 The extension reason quoted above says the same about WebMCP specifically. Table 15.1 shows what that meant in 2026. Each row is a change to the specification that could break code written against an earlier draft.

Table 15.1 — Breaking or behaviour-changing spec changes in 2026, from the commit history8:1

Date Change Pull request
5 Mar 2026 provideContext() and clearContext() removed #132
27 May 2026 modelContext getter moved from Navigator to Document #184
8 Jun 2026 registerTool() returns a promise #200
21 Jul 2026 annotations moved into a separate object #225
17 Aug 2026 executeTool() takes an object instead of a JSON string #246
30 Sep 2026 Origin-keyed agent cluster requirement removed #330
8 Oct 2026 Declarative (HTML forms) API removed from the spec “for now” #338
8 Oct 2026 UnknownError replaced with specific DOMException types #339

The browser and the draft don’t always move together. Chrome’s WebMCP documentation, updated on 7 October 2026, still says “There are two APIs you can use” and describes the declarative one; the spec removed that API the next day.14:18:2 Chapter 8 covers what the trial still ships, and Appendix D walks through migrating code written before the May move.

Still in flux: the trial and the draft

Error types. Pull request #339 replaced UnknownError with specific exception types on 8 October 2026.8:3 Chromium 156 still returns UnknownError in the cases Chapters 6 and 7 measured, so code that branches on err.name should treat both as possible for now. The declarative API. It is in Chrome’s trial and documentation, and out of the spec.14:28:4 Which improvements the extension tests. chromestatus says the extension exists to gather data on API improvements suggested by trial feedback, but doesn’t list them.9:7

Detecting what you are running on

With two trials, a flag, a moved attribute and a policy that can switch the whole API off, a single 'modelContext' in document check answers only part of the question. Listing 15.2 is a small module that answers all of it and registers tools only where that is safe.

Each field maps to something in the draft. modelContext is a [SecureContext] attribute on Document, so it exists only on HTTPS pages and on localhost. The ModelContext interface declares the three methods and three event handler attributes the module looks for. Access is gated by a policy-controlled feature named "tools", whose default allowlist is 'self'.15 The spec recommends sending Permissions-Policy: tools=() from pages that should never register tools, so a page can find the API present and still be forbidden to use it.16

The book’s companion repository (folder chapters/15-browser-support-and-standards in webmcp-book-demos) runs Listing 15.2 in Chromium 156.0.8078.4 in three configurations. With --enable-features=WebMCPTesting, the module reports all three methods, all three events and policyAllows: true, and the Trailhead search_products tool registers and shows up in getTools(). With the same flag and a Permissions-Policy: tools=() header, the API is still present but policyAllows is false. Calling registerTool() anyway is rejected with a NotAllowedError whose message reads “Access to the feature "tools" is disallowed by permissions policy.” Without the flag, document.modelContext doesn’t exist, the policy doesn’t list a "tools" feature, and the page carries on without tools. In all three cases the page itself works, which is the point.

Two caveats. First, the module asks document.permissionsPolicy and falls back to document.featurePolicy, which is the object Chromium 156 answered on in these tests. Neither is available in every engine, so a null result means “unknown”, not “allowed”. Second, a polyfill (discussed later in this chapter) defines document.modelContext on purpose, and the module will report it as available. That is the correct answer for your registration code. It tells you nothing about which agent, if any, will call the tools.

Firefox and WebKit, in their own words

Chapter 4 summarised both positions in a paragraph each. They deserve more than that, because they are the clearest statements anyone outside Google and Microsoft has made about what WebMCP is for, and because each points to a different future for the API.

Mozilla: neutral, and reopening

Dominic Farolino, one of the spec’s editors, asked Mozilla for a position on 28 May 2026. His request framed WebMCP as serving two use cases: built-in browser agents acting on a site, and in-page agents, “possibly in cross-origin iframes”, calling tools another origin explicitly exposed.3:2 Mozilla’s reviewer, Benjamin VanderSloot, replied on 1 June. His assessment is worth reading as a checklist of what a browser vendor weighs.

He starts with the benefit. The API gives websites a way to declare dedicated “lanes” for automated interaction, and “with honest participants, the benefit is twofold”: agents get a clear signal of what actions are available, and developers no longer have to design a single interface that serves both humans and automation.3:3 Then comes the risk: “in an adversarial setting there is a risk that sites will provide tools that do not match the experience of a user on the page,” whether to “tar pit automated browsers, provide prompt injection that is invisible to typical users, collect user data from the inputs of the tools, or otherwise manipulate a user’s browsing ‘agent’.” He adds a fair qualification: “it is not clear to what extent they are exacerbated by this API or if they are inherent to LLMs consuming content from and driving a browser.”3:4

Two further points carry practical weight for you. The first is the name. “The name is misleading,” he writes, because developers “(reasonably) assume the MCP spec is involved in any way. There is no MCP here.” He suggests names like “Website Tool API” or “Agent Capability API”.3:5 If the API is ever renamed, this comment is where the pressure came from. The second is openness. “As of now, use of this mechanism is restricted to browser developer’s own products and in-page agents,” and opening it up means “adding WebExtension and WebDriver BiDi integrations.”3:6 In other words, an independent agent shipped as a browser extension has no standard way to call your tools today.

His conclusion: WebMCP “introduces a potentially valuable abstraction” but “opens a surface whose real-world dynamics leave too many open questions to wholeheartedly endorse,” so he proposed neutral, with a willingness “to come back to revisit it once there is more evidence of how it will be used by sites.” The label position: neutral was applied on 5 August 2026.3:7

The story didn’t end there. Mozilla had filed a meta bug in February, “[meta] Implement a prototype WebMCP API”, which is still open.17 In August, Jake Archibald opened issue #236 in the WebMCP repository, asking whether the feature should be repositioned “as a general way to call functions in other environments”: windows, workers and other origins, with exposure to “the browser” (and through it to WebDriver or an LLM) as one more target.18 Back in the positions thread, Farolino asked whether Mozilla’s support depended on dropping the declarative API. Archibald answered that the declarative form “sounds like a reasonable idea” but shouldn’t come “instead of an imperative way to call functions between environments”. Martin Thomson added that #236 “is pretty significant here. As is naming. But this position is not really based on the declarative variant.”3:8 The editors have been working through #236 since, sketching handles such as tool.call(…) that could be passed across postMessage(); on 22 September Johann Hofmann summarised the security requirements for that model, starting with the rule that cross-origin exposure “must be opt in on the side of the tool providing origin.”18:1 On 9 October Farolino told the TAG that the editors were “working closely with Mozilla” on these changes “to gain their support”, and asked the TAG to wait for “Mozilla’s refreshed standards position.”5:2

So Mozilla’s neutral is not a resting state. It is the start of a negotiation whose likely price is an API that looks less like “tools for AI” and more like a general cross-origin function-call mechanism, with agents as one consumer among several.

WebKit: opposed, and proposing a different process

WebKit’s position, posted on 3 June 2026 and labelled position: oppose on 11 June, rests on five arguments.4:2 Chapter 4 quoted the first two: tool descriptions move the brittleness “from the DOM into the tool descriptions”, and an agent acting for a user “is, in effect, assistive technology” that a site should not single out. The remaining three are as important.

  • Unexamined risks. WebKit calls WebMCP “a new cross-origin invocation path” whose interaction with the platform’s isolation model (COOP, COEP, site isolation) is unexamined, with “no consent or reversibility model for consequential actions”. It warns that a site could over-parameterise a tool so that a helpful agent fills it in from personal data “the user never gave that site”, a pipeline the comment links to cross-site tracking.4:3
  • Not really MCP. Because the spec “does not prescribe the format in which tools are exposed”, WebKit reads WebMCP as a general mechanism for a page to register typed, callable functions, which “belongs with the platform’s existing messaging and capability mechanisms (postMessage and similar), not a parallel one.”4:4 This is the same observation that led Mozilla to #236, reaching the opposite conclusion.
  • The wrong venue. “The Machine Learning CG/WG venue is wrong for the work.” The gaps WebMCP identifies, WebKit argues, are in HTML and accessibility semantics, which belong to WHATWG and the W3C’s ARIA and Accessible Platform Architectures groups.4:5

The issue’s labels record the same objections as concerns about API design, duplication, internationalisation, portability, privacy, security, use cases and venue.4:6

When Farolino asked follow-up questions, Marcos Cáceres replied on 17 June that WebKit would not answer them point by point, because each question assumed the rest of the approach was sound. Instead WebKit set out “invariants that put users in control” (“an agent acting on a user’s behalf is assistive technology”, sites should not be told that a user relies on an agent, and the result “must not privilege those who have one”), followed by a seven-step path: set WebMCP aside, stand up “a new community group for agent-assisted user agents”, define the problem with “no solutions and no engineering, just use cases”, hold a W3C workshop, perhaps around TPAC 2026 (26–30 October, Dublin), and only then route solutions to HTML, ARIA or elsewhere.4:7

For an adopter, the practical reading is simple. No WebKit implementation is coming for the API in its current form. Safari’s entry on the implementation-status page links to the position and to nothing else.13:1 And the argument WebKit makes is not about details that a few pull requests could fix. It questions whether a separate tool layer should exist at all.

The TAG review

The TAG’s early review of the Community Group work was filed on 11 June 2026. Marcos Cáceres suggested expediting it, since a proposal to add WebMCP to a Working Group charter was already on the table, and W3C staff agreed.5:3 On 10 July the TAG labelled it “Progress: in progress” and set six focus areas as pending: API design, web architecture, security, privacy, accessibility and internationalisation. It also added the label that sums up the politics: “Missing: Multi-stakeholder support.”5:4

The public thread shows where the argument has settled. After a TAG breakout meeting in August, Farolino reported that the question that “keeps coming up over and over” was why WebMCP is shaped as an explicit capability layer rather than “more HTML semantics”. He asked that any negative resolution on those grounds come with evidence that semantics would be a sufficient alternative.5:5 Two adopters weighed in. Yoav Weiss, writing “as someone deploying WebMCP (under an Origin Trial in various Chromium browsers) to a large number of storefronts”, listed the Shopify storefront tools in use (browsing collections, managing orders, searching the catalogue, showing product variants, searching store policies) and said he didn’t “see a feasible declarative alternative to the imperative tools that agents can call.”5:6 A second commenter cited his company’s public benchmark, which reports UI actuation using about 5–10 times the tokens and cost per task, and running 4–5 times slower, than WebMCP. That figure is the vendor’s own claim, and this book has not reproduced it.5:7 TAG members asked people not to read too much into draft notes. Marcos Cáceres reminded participants that notes shared privately “do not represent the consensus of the TAG in any way, shape, or form.”5:8

The latest public word from the TAG, on 6 October, is that the review is “taking a bit longer than usual.” On 9 October the editors asked the TAG to hold its position until after Mozilla’s refreshed position and after TPAC.5:9

Still in flux: the review outcomes

The TAG’s conclusion. No position had been published as of 15 October 2026, and the editors have asked for it to wait until after TPAC.5:10 Mozilla’s position. It is being renegotiated around issue #236, and it could change the TAG’s “Missing: Multi-stakeholder support” label.18:25:11 WebKit’s position. It is oppose, and the issue is closed.4:8

Who consumes WebMCP today

Exposing tools is only half of the system. Something has to call them. The project’s implementation-status page is the only list of consumers in one place, and it is the project’s own claim rather than each vendor’s.13:2 As of 15 October 2026 it lists:

  • Chrome: the origin trial, live from Chrome 149. The trial describes itself as letting websites “register tools for use by agents hosted by the site or in Chrome.”13:39:8
  • Edge: the origin trial, live in Edge 150.13:4
  • Brave: “Experimental support is added to Leo AI chat.”13:5 The Brave issue behind it was first closed on 7 July 2026 but has been reopened twice since, most recently on 7 October, and it is open as of 15 October 2026. On 1 October a Brave engineer wrote that the feature is “flagged on in Nightly at the moment”. The issue’s test plan turns on brave://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and expects a “tools pill” in Leo’s sidebar when a page offers tools.19
  • ChatGPT Desktop: “WebMCP is supported in ChatGPT Desktop.”13:6 OpenAI’s earlier agentic browser, ChatGPT Atlas, is gone. OpenAI announced its retirement on 9 July 2026, alongside a desktop app with its own built-in browser, and its help centre now says that “ChatGPT Atlas has been retired and no longer receives updates.”20
  • Meta Ray-Ban Display: support for web apps is “coming soon”, letting Meta AI on the glasses call tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(). It is off by default and enabled per device.13:7
  • Firefox and Safari: links to their positions, plus Mozilla’s Bugzilla meta bug.13:8

Then there are extensions. chromestatus notes that the Chrome Web Store “features about 9 different extensions with WebMCP on their title and 4* or more ratings”.9:9 MCP-B’s Rook is one such agent extension.21 Remember Mozilla’s point, though: there is no standard extension or WebDriver API for calling page tools yet, so each of these depends on Chromium-specific plumbing.3:9 On the automation side, W3C staff have floated giving the Browser Testing and Tools Working Group the job of “enabling MCP support bidirectional WebDriver protocol for browser automation.”6:1

For planning, the order of confidence is: Chromium browsers with the trial (verifiable today with a token), Brave behind a flag, then vendors whose support is stated only on the status page. Test against what you can run, and treat the rest as upside.

Community libraries

Long before the browsers, the community had built WebMCP-shaped libraries. Chapter 4 described MCP-B’s role in the API’s history. Today its packages are the most widely used way to try WebMCP outside a Chromium trial. Each of the three main packages was at version 6.0.3 on 15 October 2026, published the day before, under the MIT licence:22

Package Description (from the npm registry)
@mcp-b/global “W3C Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) API polyfill. Let AI agents like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini interact with your website via document.modelCont[ext]…”
@mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill “Vendored upstream WebMCP polyfill plus temporary declarative tools”
usewebmcp “Standalone React hooks for strict core WebMCP tool registration with document.modelContext”

The documentation site registers a live tool with document.modelContext.registerTool() on its own home page and suggests calling it through “the Rook extension or Chrome’s native WebMCP support.”21:1 The packages live in the WebMCP-org/npm-packages repository, which describes them as “Transport layers, React hooks, and browser tools for the Model Context Protocol”.23 Chapter 10 uses usewebmcp in the Trailhead React app.

Three cautions apply to any library that tracks a moving draft:

  1. A polyfill is a second implementation with its own schedule. When the spec dropped the declarative API on 8 October, the polyfill kept “temporary declarative tools”.8:522:1 That is a reasonable choice for users, but it means the polyfill and the draft can disagree.
  2. Version numbers move as fast as the spec. All three packages were republished on 14 October 2026, the day before this chapter was checked. Pin exact versions, and read the changelog before upgrading.
  3. A polyfill cannot create consumers. It gives your page a document.modelContext to register on. Calls still need an agent that knows how to reach it, such as a matching extension. The detection code in Listing 15.2 can’t tell native support from a polyfill, and for registration purposes it doesn’t need to.

From Community Group to Working Group

What a Working Group would change

The W3C’s rule is short: “Community Groups are for incubation. The Recommendation Track is for standardization.” A technology that gains traction in a CG normally moves to a Working Group (WG) to become a standard, and the CG agreements are written so that participants’ patent commitments carry over.1:2 For adopters, three things change when a WG takes over a specification:

  • Patent commitments. The W3C designed its CG agreements for “continuity of IPR commitments” when a Working Group adopts a CG specification, so the move itself is meant to be smooth.1:3 A WG brings the W3C Patent Policy with it; the draft charter below has a Patent Policy section.24
  • Horizontal review. The draft Agentic Web WG charter, discussed below, requires review for accessibility, internationalisation, privacy and security, and by the TAG, “during each major standards-track document transition”.24:1
  • Interoperability as a bar. To advance beyond Candidate Recommendation, the draft charter expects “at least two independent interoperable implementations of every feature defined in the specification, where interoperability can be verified by passing open test suites.”24:2 The WebMCP draft already links a test suite on wpt.fyi from its header.2:2 Today, every implementation of WebMCP is built on Chromium.

The last point is the political core of this chapter. Two Chromium-based browsers are not two independent implementations, and the two engines that are independent of Chromium are respectively neutral and opposed. A Working Group would not make WebMCP a standard by itself. It would set a bar that, as of October 2026, nobody has a plan to meet.

What happened in 2026

The question of a WG came up within a day of the positions being requested. On 28 May 2026, the WebKit engineer who would post WebKit’s position a week later opened issue #192, noting that “Community Groups do not create W3C standards” and asking whether WebMCP should move to the WG.25 W3C staff supported an early rechartering of the Web Machine Learning WG to take it in, and on 9 June a pull request proposed adding WebMCP to that group’s charter “as a tentative deliverable.”6:225:1 The WebML WG is chartered until 30 April 2027.26

That route ran into trouble almost immediately. WebKit’s position, published the same month, called the machine-learning venue wrong for the work.4:9 On 18 June the author of #192 clarified that they had proposed discussing the move, not supporting it: “We think WebML WG is the incorrect working group, but WebMCP should be part of some working group.”25:2 On 13 August the WG recorded a resolution that it “has reviewed the charter proposal and approves the direction. WebKit position duly noted.” Marcos Cáceres replied that it was “baffling how you can record a resolution when a member of the working group has objected,” and Apple disputed the minutes the next day.25:3 The same day, on the charter pull request, Cáceres recorded “that Apple is opposed to this going working group. Expect a formal objection if this is merged.” He added: “We'd be open to discussing a different venue at the W3C and doing this properly from first principles (i.e., some new agentic web CG/WG).”6:3

A formal objection is not just a strong comment. Under the W3C Process, Formal Objections “receive formal consideration and a formal response”. If the Team cannot resolve one through investigation and mediation, it goes to the W3C Council.27 Any charter that names WebMCP and draws an objection from Apple faces that procedure.

On 28 September W3C staff changed course. The “latest thinking,” wrote Philippe le Hégaret, the W3C’s Chartering Facilitator,28 on the charter pull request, “is to have a working group dedicated to develop specifications that facilitate web pages and applications to be leveraged by LLMs and AI agents,” while the WebML WG would “stay focused on developing APIs for enabling efficient machine learning inference in the browser.”6:4 The same day a charter proposal for an Agentic Web Working Group appeared, stated to “replace the previous thinking”, and on 13 October the WebML pull request was closed.7:16:5

The Agentic Web Working Group charter

The draft charter’s mission is “to develop specifications that facilitate web pages and applications to be leveraged by LLMs and AI agents.” Its scope covers describing site capabilities and context for agents, representing agent identity and delegation, transparency about agent interactions, “expressing permissions, policies, and constraints on agent actions”, and guidance for authors. It explicitly excludes model APIs, crawler controls, bot detection and agent-to-server communications, among others.24:3 Its one named normative deliverable is WebMCP, “adopted from the Web Machine Learning Community Group”.24:4

It is still very much a draft. On 15 October 2026 the chairs, dates, team contact and timeline were template placeholders, and the deliverables section still carried both template options: whether the group intends to stop at Candidate Recommendation or go on to Recommendation.24:5 The W3C announced the start of charter refinement on 1 October and estimated that it “will last until approximately 10 November 2026.”28:1 The Process Document requires that phase to last at least 28 days, and an Advisory Committee review follows it.27:1 The strategy issue lists the TAG review, the accessibility considerations and a threat model among its “known or potential areas of concern”.7:2

The draft’s scope is broader than WebMCP, and in places it echoes the critics. Agent transparency and “permissions, policies, and constraints on agent actions” are close to the consent and control questions WebKit raised.24:64:10 Whether WebKit would accept this group as the “new agentic web CG/WG” Apple said it was open to, and whether it would accept WebMCP as a starting deliverable rather than a proposal to set aside, is not on the public record. Farolino’s answer to WebKit’s call for a new group was: “I have no objection to moving WebMCP exactly as-is to such a WG.”25:4

The paths, and what each means for you

Figure 15.2 lays out the routes visible on 15 October 2026.

  • The Agentic Web WG charters with WebMCP in scope. The specification moves to the Recommendation Track with patent commitments and horizontal review. Expect a stream of changes from TAG and accessibility review, and expect the interoperability bar to keep the specification at Candidate Recommendation, or below it, until a second engine implements it. For your code, nothing changes on charter day. Changes come later, through review.
  • The charter is delayed or WebMCP is taken out of it. WebMCP stays a CG report. Chromium-based browsers can keep running trials or ship it, but it would remain a Chromium-only feature with no standards-track commitments.
  • The API is reshaped before either happens. If #236 succeeds, the core becomes a general cross-environment function-call mechanism, and agents become one consumer.18:3 Mozilla might move off neutral; WebKit’s objection to a separate agent-facing layer would remain.3:104:11 Your tools would survive as functions with names, descriptions and schemas, but registration and invocation code would change.

None of these paths removes the advice from Chapter 4. Build tools as thin wrappers over logic your interface already uses, feature-detect at run time, and treat WebMCP as a progressive enhancement. The cost of following a breaking change is then a few lines in one module.

Still in flux: the venue

Charter refinement. It is expected to end around 10 November 2026; extensions are announced on the strategy issue.28:27:3 Apple’s response to the new charter. Apple threatened a formal objection to the WebML route. Its view of the Agentic Web WG draft is not on the public record as of 15 October 2026.6:67:4 Recommendation or not. The draft charter has not yet chosen whether the group will aim for full Recommendation.24:7

Keeping this chapter current yourself

Every fact in this chapter has a date on it, and several will have changed before you read this. The responsible way to rely on any of them is to re-check them on a schedule. Listing 15.3 does that. It reads seven primary sources, extracts one status from each, saves a snapshot, and reports what changed since the last run.

A few design choices are worth explaining. The script reads GitHub issue pages rather than the GitHub REST API, because unauthenticated API calls are rate-limited, and a weekly job shared by a team quickly hits that limit. It takes only the issue’s current labels block, not the label events in the timeline, so a label that was added and later removed doesn’t show up as current. The test suite has a case for exactly that, using the TAG’s since-removed “Progress: untriaged” label. Each source fails independently: a page that times out becomes an { error } entry rather than a crash. And the exit code is 2 when something changed, so a CI job can open an issue or send a message.

Here is the snapshot it produced when this chapter was checked:

Run it weekly. The fields that matter most for planning are chromestatus.trialThrough (renew your tokens before it passes), edgeTrial, and any change to the mozilla, webkit and tag labels. A spec date change on its own is routine; read the commit titles it points to.

What this means for your product

  • Plan for Chromium only, and design for everyone. Today’s reachable audience for WebMCP is users of Chromium-based browsers whose sites carry trial tokens, plus agents that consume tools through Chromium. Your site must work fully without tools in every other browser, which progressive enhancement gives you for free.
  • Put the trial on someone’s calendar. Chrome’s trial runs through Chrome 162, Edge’s through 30 March 2027, and an extension means new tokens. Assign an owner for registration, renewal and the token in your deployment configuration.
  • Budget for churn. Eight behaviour-changing spec changes in 2026 is the baseline (Table 15.1). Keep WebMCP code in one module, pin library versions, and run the Chapter 14 tests against each new Chromium release.
  • Treat standards politics as a risk, not a verdict. Neutral can become positive if the API is reshaped, and a Working Group would add review and stability. Opposition from WebKit means no Safari support for this design. Neither changes whether well-designed tools help your users in browsers that have them.
  • Feed the process. Google’s trial asks for feedback on the API shape, and the TAG thread shows that deployment data carries weight: Shopify storefront tools were cited as an argument.12:25:12 Real usage from your product is the most persuasive input you can give.

Chapter summary

  • WebMCP is a Draft Community Group Report (15 October 2026) of the W3C Web Machine Learning CG. It is not a W3C standard and not on the Standards Track. Community Groups incubate; only a Working Group can standardise.
  • Chrome’s origin trial runs from Chrome 149, originally through 156 and since 28 September 2026 extended through 162. Edge’s trial runs in Edge 150 until 30 March 2027. Both accept third-party tokens. Tokens go in a meta tag, an HTTP header or, for third parties, an external script, and an extension means renewing them.
  • Trials exist to change APIs. In 2026 the spec removed provideContext(), moved modelContext to Document, made registerTool() return a promise, removed the declarative API and changed its error types. The trial and the documentation don’t always match the draft.
  • Feature detection should cover the secure context, the methods and events, the "tools" permissions policy and the old navigator surface. In Chromium 156, a page under Permissions-Policy: tools=() still sees the API, but calls are rejected with NotAllowedError.
  • Mozilla is neutral: tools are useful “lanes”, but adversarial sites, a misleading name and a closed set of consumers leave “too many open questions”. It is renegotiating around a more general cross-environment function-call API (#236).
  • WebKit is opposed: agents are assistive technology and should not be singled out, the tool layer duplicates HTML and ARIA, the risks are unexamined and the venue is wrong. It proposes starting over in a new group, from use cases.
  • The TAG review, open since June 2026, is labelled “Missing: Multi-stakeholder support”, with six focus areas pending and no position yet.
  • Consumers listed today: Chrome and Edge trials, Brave Leo (experimental), ChatGPT Desktop (per the project’s status page; ChatGPT Atlas was retired) and Meta Ray-Ban Display (“coming soon”), plus Chromium extensions. Community packages (@mcp-b/global, @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill, usewebmcp, all at 6.0.3) track the draft quickly, but on their own schedule.
  • A move into the WebML Working Group was dropped after Apple warned of a formal objection. A new Agentic Web Working Group charter naming WebMCP is in refinement until about 10 November 2026. Standardisation would still require two independent interoperable implementations.
  • Re-check status on a schedule. Listing 15.3 snapshots seven primary sources and flags changes.

Chapter 16 turns from the platform to the business: which journeys to expose first, how to keep the agent a guest on your site, and how to measure what agent-driven traffic is worth.

Part VI · Strategy and the future

Chapter 16: Product and Business Implications

“Tools execute on your webpage visibly, so users gain trust that tasks are completed as expected. This also keeps your brand and human-centered design choices intact.”

— Chrome for Developers, “WebMCP”1

The question on Kari’s whiteboard

Trailhead’s product team meets on Monday mornings in a room above the warehouse in Lillestrøm. This Monday, Kari, who runs product, has written one question on the whiteboard: What do we ship for agents, and how will we know it worked?

Jonas, the front-end lead, has spent the last month on the earlier chapters of this book. He has a branch where search_products and add_to_cart are registered with document.modelContext, and he can show an agent finding a two-person tent under 4,000 NOK and putting it in the cart in four tool calls instead of forty clicks. Kari is impressed, and she is also the person who has to explain the work to the rest of the company. So her questions are not about AbortSignal. Will agents find us? Which journeys first? Do we lose the customer to the assistant? What do we measure? Who owns the descriptions? What happens if the standard changes or never ships?

This chapter is for the people in that room. Most of it can be read without the code, and the code that is here is short: a catalog that treats tools as product surface, a budget check for CI, a measurement wrapper, and an attribution helper, all for Trailhead. Every listing runs, and the tests for them live in the book’s demos repository.2

Agent-readiness is not the new SEO (yet)

The comparison comes up in every planning meeting about agents. Twenty-five years ago companies learned to describe their pages for crawlers, and now they will learn to describe their features for agents. Some of that holds. A WebMCP tool’s name and description are text written for a machine reader, and their quality decides whether the reader uses your feature correctly. Chrome’s guidance on descriptions reads like a copywriting brief: “use verbs that describe exactly what happens”, say “what the tool does and when to use it”, and “rely on positive language” rather than lists of limitations.3 Agents also choose between tools, and Chrome’s evaluation guide lists “Agent fails to select the correct tool” as the first failure mode to test for.4 Writing good tool copy is a skill worth having in-house, as SEO copy once was.

The analogy breaks at the step that made SEO valuable: discovery. A search engine indexes your pages before anyone visits them, and that index sends you visitors you didn’t have. WebMCP has no equivalent. Chrome’s own documentation lists it as a limitation: “Clients and browsers must visit a site directly to know if it has callable tools.”1:1 Chrome’s comparison with MCP says the same thing from the other side. MCP’s discovery happens through “agent-specific registration flows”, while WebMCP’s tools are “registered on the web page during the user’s visit.”5 There is no central registry of WebMCP sites, no crawler that reads registerTool() calls and no ranking for tools.

This is a design choice, not an oversight. The explainer considered “static declarative manifests”, tools listed in a file such as the Web App Manifest, and set them aside because they “prevent web developers from dynamically adding, updating, or removing tools based on the active page state or user authentication status”. It left the door open: static declarations could be “layered on in the future”.6 The supplementary explainer for service workers, which asks how an agent could use a site the user doesn’t have open, discusses discovery directly. It lists possible mechanisms (“installable PWAs”, “web search”, “curated site directories”, “direct links”) and floats the idea of sites advertising “high-level descriptions of the capabilities they offer” in a manifest or in page markup, so that crawlers and directories can recommend them. It also calls discovery “a complex topic which goes beyond the scope of this explainer”.7

Table 16.1 — Where the SEO analogy holds and where it breaks (October 2026)

Search engine optimization Agent-readiness with WebMCP
Who reads your text A crawler, ahead of time An agent, during the user’s visit
What brings the user The index sends new visitors The user is already on your site
What you optimize Pages, titles, structured data Tool names, descriptions, schemas, results
Central registry or ranking Yes, run by each search engine None defined
How you measure Impressions, clicks, rankings Tool calls, outcomes, assisted conversions
What it mostly grows Acquisition Conversion and task completion

The business consequence is the most important sentence in this chapter. WebMCP, as specified today, converts visits you already have. It doesn’t bring new ones. An agent reaches Trailhead’s tools because the customer opened Trailhead, typed its address, followed a link or clicked a search result. That changes the investment case. You are not buying a new channel, you are cutting friction and failure out of the sessions you already pay to acquire. If agents arriving through actuation today fail half-way through your checkout, every one of those failures is a lost conversion you already paid for. That is a measurable cost, and it is where the case for WebMCP is strongest.

Still in flux: discovery

Manifests and directories. Static tool declarations were rejected as the primary mechanism, but the explainer says they could be added on top later, and the service-worker explainer discusses manifest fields and capability descriptions for crawlers and directories. Neither is in the specification.6:17:1 Sites that aren’t open. Letting agents call tools on sites the user doesn’t have open is an open question in the main explainer, which points to the service-worker proposal for it.8 Chapter 17 covers what that would change.

Choosing the first journeys

If WebMCP converts visits you already have, the first journeys to expose are the ones where those visits fail today and where success is worth the most. Chrome frames the work around critical user journeys (CUJs), defined as “a user’s path to accomplish a goal, including any required context”, and its use-case guide walks through shopping, repeat purchases and form filling.9 For retail it suggests tools such as search_products(), add_to_wishlist() and a refine_search() for price ranges, and for repeat purchases a get_order_history() tool.9:1 The explainer’s own shopping scenario has an agent fetch product listings, filter them against the user’s request and call a second tool to update the store’s grid, so the shopper sees the agent’s choice on the page.10

Four kinds of journey account for most of the candidates on a typical site.

  • Search and filter. Finding things in a catalogue, a timetable or an inventory. Read-only, high volume, and painful to actuate when filters are custom widgets. These are the safest place to start.
  • Configure. Choosing options, sizes, dates, seats or plans: the multi-step forms where agents guess at ambiguous fields. Chrome’s example is a tool that distinguishes “a full name versus a separate first and last name”.1:2
  • Book and buy. Adding to a cart, reserving, checking out. High value, and consequential at the final step.
  • Support. Filing a claim, finding an order, opening a ticket. Chrome’s use-case guide includes a warranty claim, and its overview puts “Help your customers get support” first among its examples.9:21:3

Rank candidates on a few questions, in roughly this order.

  1. How badly does actuation fail here today? If agents already complete the journey reliably, a tool adds little. Custom date pickers, steppers, infinite scroll and multi-step modals are the usual culprits.
  2. What is a completion worth? An abandoned checkout costs more than an abandoned “About us” page.
  3. Can the existing code be reused? The explainer’s goal is that “any task that a user can accomplish through a page’s UI can be turned into a tool by reusing much of the page’s existing client-side code.”11 Chrome is equally clear about the opposite case: if a site is highly complex, “you likely need to refactor or add JavaScript to handle application and interface state.”1:4 A journey whose logic is tangled into components costs more to expose.
  4. What happens if the agent gets it wrong? A wrong search is free. A wrong order is a refund, a support call and a customer who won’t try it again. Consequential steps are possible, but they need the confirmation design from Chapter 13.
  5. How many tools does it need? Chrome notes that while there is no maximum, “each tool takes up part of the context window and adds to the time for completion”, and that overlapping tools make it harder for the agent to choose.3:1 Journeys that need a small, distinct set of tools ship faster and test more easily.

For Trailhead, Figure 16.1 gives an order that Kari can defend. Product search and comparison come first: read-only, heavily used and backed by code the React app already has (Chapter 10 builds them in React). The cart comes next, because adding an item is reversible and the cart badge makes the result visible. Checkout comes third, as a tool that opens the checkout summary and stops. The customer places the order with their own click, which is how the canonical checkout tool is defined throughout this book. Order status and returns come later. Order status is already served by the backend MCP server from Chapter 3, and returns involve policy questions the team hasn’t answered yet.

Table 16.2 — Trailhead’s first release

Journey Tool Annotation Why now
Discover search_products readOnlyHint Custom filter widgets defeat actuation; no risk
Decide compare_products readOnlyHint The comparison table is hard to read from pixels
Buy add_to_cart, get_cart — / readOnlyHint Reversible, visible in the cart badge
Buy checkout consequentialHint Opens the summary only; the customer clicks “Place order”
Support get_order_status — Later on the page; already on the backend MCP server (Chapter 3)

Five tools is a deliberate number. It is small enough for every one to have an owner and an eval suite, and it covers a complete journey from search to a placed order. A team that exposes fifty tools in its first release is making the agent’s choice harder and giving itself fifty things to test.

Keeping the agent a guest

The strategic fear behind many agent discussions is disintermediation: the assistant becomes the storefront, your site becomes a supplier behind it, and your brand shrinks to a line in a chat transcript. WebMCP’s authors share the fear and designed against it. One of the explainer’s stated goals is “Prevent web content disintermediation”, which it explains as preventing “disintermediation of web apps by backend integrations by adapting front-ends for use by agents, rather than replacing them”. Its non-goals include “replacement of human interfaces”: “The human web interface remains primary; agent tools augment rather than replace user interaction.”11:1 Chrome puts it more sharply in the line quoted in Chapter 4: “Instead of your application being a guest within an agent, the agent is a guest on your platform.”5:1

That framing is accurate about the mechanics, and it is worth being precise about what it does and doesn’t give you.

What it gives you is presence. Tools are ephemeral and live in your tab: “Once the user navigates away from your site or closes the tab, the agent cannot access your site or take actions.”5:2 Your tool runs your code and can update your interface while the user watches. That’s why Chrome says tools “execute on your webpage visibly” and keep “your brand and human-centered design choices intact”.1:5 If search_products renders its results in Trailhead’s own grid, the customer sees Trailhead’s photography, prices and reviews, not a reformatted list in a chat bubble.

What it doesn’t give you is control over how the agent uses what you return. An agent can call your tools, take the JSON and compare it with three other stores. Chrome’s use-case guide describes exactly that: a shopper asks for “the best prices for the products on my shopping list at two or three local stores”, and each store’s tools feed the comparison.9:3 Structured results make you easier to compare, and in a commodity category easier to compare can mean easier to replace.

So the brand decisions are about what you put in the tool contract and what you keep on the page.

  • Show, don’t just return. Have every tool that finds something put it on screen. Chapter 5’s rule, “the user sees what the agent found”, is as much a brand rule as a UX rule.
  • Return what helps the agent decide honestly. Ratings, stock, delivery times, the reasons to buy from you. If your advantage is next-day delivery to Tromsø, put it in the result. If it’s only visible in a banner image, the agent won’t see it.
  • Keep consequential steps on your page. The spec’s consequentialHint signals that a tool performs a significant action, “such as booking a flight or transferring money”, so that clients “can selectively enforce mandatory user confirmation prompts”.12 Trailhead goes further: the checkout tool opens the summary, and only the customer’s click places the order. Your confirmation screen, your terms, your upsells, your brand.
  • Don’t over-ask. The spec’s privacy section describes “privacy leakage through over-parameterization”: tools designed with many optional parameters so that helpful agents fill them from the user’s personal context, creating “a personalization-to-fingerprinting pipeline”.13 Asking an agent for age, location and previous purchases “for better recommendations” is the kind of thing that will cost you trust when someone notices, and the spec has named it as an attack.

Tools are product surface

Trust in your tools is a brand asset, and the spec explains why it is fragile. Section 6.3.2, “Misrepresentation of Intent”, starts from the fact that “there is no guarantee that a WebMCP tool’s declared intent matches its actual behavior”, and it lists two causes. One is fraud. The other is “accidental misalignment”: “poorly written descriptions, outdated documentation, or inherent imprecision in natural language.”14 A description that says “adds to cart” while the code also applies a promotional bundle is a misrepresentation, even if nobody meant it.

The fix is organizational as much as technical. Trailhead keeps every agent-facing string in one file, reviewed like product copy, with an owner and an eval suite per tool (Listing 16.1).

Three details matter. The descriptions say what the tool does and what it returns, in positive language, as Chrome recommends.3:2 The checkout description states the boundary (“this tool never pays”), because a description is the only promise the agent can read. And as const satisfies keeps the literal names as types, so that the registration code in Listing 16.4 can’t register a tool that isn’t in the catalog.

Measuring agent-driven conversion

Kari’s second question was how they will know it worked. The good news is that WebMCP is unusually measurable. Every tool call runs your own execute callback in your own page, so you can see each call, its outcome and its timing with ordinary front-end analytics. The bad news is that you will know that an agent called you, but not which agent or why.

What the platform tells you

Look at what your callback receives. In the specification’s IDL, execute gets the input object and a ToolExecuteCallbackOptions dictionary whose only member is the signal.15 There is no caller identity, no agent name, no model and no conversation. The spec defines agents broadly (its introduction says tools can be invoked by “agents, browser’s agents, and assistive technologies”), and it doesn’t ask any of them to identify themselves to the page.16

The ModelContext object also fires two events: toolactivated, “dispatched … when the execution of a tool begins”, and toolcancel, dispatched when an execution is cancelled. Both carry only a toolName.17 In our tests on 15 October 2026, Chromium 156 with the WebMCP testing flag fired toolactivated on document.modelContext for each in-page executeTool() call, in the same order as the calls.2:1 The events are useful for a lightweight counter that doesn’t touch tool code, but they can’t tell you whether a call succeeded.

The declarative API, which Chapter 8 covers and which was removed from the specification in October 2026, adds an agentInvoked member to SubmitEvent so form handlers can tell agent submissions from human ones.18 The imperative API has no equivalent because it doesn’t need one: a call to execute is an agent call.

Recording outcomes

The most useful single metric is the outcome of each call. Chapter 5 established the rule of returning recoverable failures as values, and Chapter 11 settled their shape for the whole book: { status, code, message }. The status says who acts next: 'error' for something the agent can fix, like an unknown SKU; 'needs_input' when only the user knows the answer; 'refused' when a rule says no, as with an out-of-stock item (code OUT_OF_STOCK); and 'cancelled_by_user' when the person declined in the page’s own UI. Exceptions are only for real faults. That convention makes outcomes easy to classify. Listing 16.2 wraps any tool and reports one record per call, without changing what the agent receives.

Each outcome starts a different conversation. A falling ok rate after a release means a description or schema regressed, and your eval suite should have caught it. A rising error rate points the same way: agents are calling the tool with arguments it can’t use. A rising refused rate with one dominant code (OUT_OF_STOCK, say) is a merchandising problem, not an engineering one. needs_input and cancelled_by_user show how often the person had to step in. Threw is a bug. Aborted means the caller aborted the call’s signal, so the agent never sees a result even if your code ran on; Chapter 6 covers what that does to your code. It isn’t a result status: a person who declines in your own UI shows up as cancelled_by_user. Durations tell you where agents wait, and Chrome’s best practices remind you that the interface should be updated once the function completes, because “agents may rely on the interface to plan next steps”.3:3

Note what the record leaves out: the input. The tool name, outcome, code and duration are enough for every metric in this chapter. Logging arguments means logging whatever the agent drew from the user’s context, and that is exactly the data the over-parameterization warning is about.13:1 If you need inputs for debugging, sample them, strip them of personal data and keep them out of your marketing warehouse.

From calls to conversions

Tool metrics tell you whether the tools work. Conversion is a business number, and it needs to be joined to orders. Trailhead takes the simplest defensible approach. It remembers which tools succeeded in the current tab session and attaches that list to the order when the customer places it (Listing 16.3).

sessionStorage is scoped to the tab, which matches WebMCP’s own scope: tools belong to a document in a tab, and so does the assistance. An order placed in a tab where the agent searched and added to the cart is agent-assisted. An order placed in a fresh tab is not. Listing 16.4 connects the pieces: the catalog decides what is registered, the wrapper measures it, and successful calls are noted for attribution.

The execute property delegates to the current handler instead of capturing it. The explainer’s best practices point out that a tool’s implementation can change: as long as the name, description and schema stay accurate, the callback can hand off to code the application changes over time, and the tool doesn’t need to be registered again.19 Changing the description is different, and the organizational section below comes back to it.

Figure 16.2 shows the resulting funnel, and Table 16.3 lists the metrics Trailhead reports weekly.

Table 16.3 — Agent metrics Trailhead tracks

Metric From Question it answers
Calls per tool, per day Listing 16.2 Is anyone using it? Which tools do agents reach for?
Outcome mix (ok, Chapter 11’s four statuses, threw, aborted) Listing 16.2 Does the tool work? Did a release regress it?
Top refused, error and needs_input codes Listing 16.2 What blocks agents: stock, input, policy?
Median and slow-tail duration Listing 16.2 Where do agents and customers wait?
Assisted order rate and value Listing 16.3 Do sessions with agent help end in orders?
Checkout opened → order placed Listings 16.2–16.3 Do customers confirm what agents prepare?

Two cautions belong in the report next to these numbers. First, assisted is not caused. A customer who uses an agent may be a more determined buyer to begin with, so compare assisted sessions with similar unassisted ones before claiming a lift, and run a holdout (tools off for a sample of sessions) if the decision is big enough. Second, today’s numbers are an origin-trial sample. Only users whose browser runs WebMCP and whose agent consumes it will reach your tools at all. The project’s implementation-status page lists Chrome and Edge trials, experimental support in Brave’s Leo, support in ChatGPT Desktop and a “coming soon” integration for Meta’s Ray-Ban Display glasses.20 Treat early volumes as a signal of where the tools work and where they don’t, not as a market forecast.

Pricing and policy questions

WebMCP doesn’t change your pricing, but it surfaces pricing and policy questions that were easy to postpone while agents only clicked. None of them has a standard answer, and most need a decision from someone above the front-end team.

Will agents see the same prices as people? They should. A tool runs in the user’s session and reads the same data as the page, so the natural design shows the same price. Agent-only prices that the page doesn’t show are the “declared intent versus actual behavior” gap the spec warns about.14:1 If you do want agent-specific offers, make them visible on the page the user is looking at.

Do you welcome price comparison? Chrome’s best practices assume you do: tools “should allow for reasonable repetition, such as for price comparison”, and a rate-limited tool should “return a meaningful error or advise the user to manually take on the task.”3:4 If your business depends on not being compared, WebMCP makes that harder to maintain, though agents could already compare prices by reading your pages.

What do your terms of service say about automation? Many sites’ terms were written to discourage scraping and bots. Browser agents already actuate those sites on users’ behalf. A WebMCP tool is a sanctioned path, and the terms and the tools should agree. It makes little sense to register add_to_cart while your terms forbid automated purchasing.

How autonomous do you allow it to be? WebMCP’s design assumes a person is present. Chrome describes the API as “primarily designed for local browser workflows with a human in the loop”, and the explainer lists “fully autonomous workflows” as a non-goal.1:611:2 Your policy can rely on that design. Consequential steps wait for a click, and a session with nobody watching gets nothing it couldn’t get from your public pages.

Who is responsible when it goes wrong? If an agent orders the wrong tent, is it the agent’s mistake, your description’s or the customer’s? The spec describes the opposite worry too, malicious tools designed so that a harmful action “can be attributed to the agent”.14:2 Precise descriptions, values for recoverable failures, a confirmation on your own page and an order history that records which steps a tool prepared are the evidence you will want if that conversation ever happens.

What about content you don’t control? Product reviews and Q&A are user-generated, and a review can contain instructions aimed at an agent. The spec’s untrustedContentHint exists for this. It marks a result whose payload “requires heightened security handling”, and Chrome recommends it for tools that return user-generated or externally sourced content.2122 Chapter 12 covers the threat model. The business point is that a tool returning reviews needs a security review before it ships.

WebMCP and backend MCP in one plan

The last strategy question is whether WebMCP replaces Trailhead’s backend MCP server from Chapter 3. It doesn’t, and the explainer says so: WebMCP “is designed to complement, not replace, existing backend-focused protocols like MCP.”11:3 Chrome’s comparison guide offers the clearest way to explain the split to a non-technical audience: “MCP is help call center and WebMCP is the in-store expert.” MCP is persistent and “available on any platform at any time”. WebMCP is ephemeral, tab-bound and “available only on your website”. Chrome’s recommendation is to use both: “manage core logic with MCP” as the platform-agnostic service layer, and “build a contextual UI with WebMCP” for in-browser work while the user has your site open.5:3

For Trailhead the division looks like Figure 16.3. The backend MCP server exposes search_products and get_order_status, the things an assistant might need when the customer is nowhere near the site (“where is my order?”). The page exposes the full journey, from search to the checkout summary, because that journey benefits from the customer’s session, cart and eyes. Three choices keep the two surfaces from drifting apart.

  • One implementation, two adapters. Both surfaces call the same catalog service. The WebMCP tool adds the page update and the confirmation; the MCP tool adds authentication and pagination.
  • The same name and schema where the tool overlaps. search_products takes the same query, category, maxPrice and inStockOnly in both places, so one set of evals and one description review covers both.
  • Different boundaries where the context differs. The backend server has no checkout tool. Purchases need the customer’s confirmation, and the page is where that confirmation lives.

Who owns the tools

Kari’s last question, who owns all this, is the one most teams get wrong, because a tool looks like code and so gets owned like code. A tool definition has at least four parts, and they belong to different people.

  • The name and description are copy. The model reads them, and they decide whether a tool gets called. They need the care you give to checkout microcopy, and someone with a product or content role should approve changes.
  • The input schema and result shape are an API contract. Engineering owns them, with the usual review for breaking changes.
  • The evals are the acceptance test for both. Chrome’s guide says that before releasing tools into production “you must confirm agents understand when to call the tool, how to execute it, and what answers are acceptable”, and that classic deterministic tests should still cover everything that doesn’t talk to the model.4:1 Chapter 14 builds Trailhead’s suites.
  • The annotations and exposure (readOnlyHint, consequentialHint, untrustedContentHint, exposedTo) are security decisions. They belong in the same review as any change to who can do what on the site.22:1

A change to the copy is also a deployment event. A tool’s name, description and schema are read into the model’s context when the agent observes the tool. To change them you unregister the tool and register it again, and agents that watch for toolchange events refresh their lists.19:1 So a description edit should go through the same eval run as a code change, and Trailhead’s CI enforces the mechanical part with Listing 16.5.

The numbers come from Chrome’s tool-security guidance, which recommends 500 characters per tool description, 150 per parameter description and 30 per tool or parameter name, and 1,500 per tool output. Chrome marks them as recommendations that may change and says specific limits “may be added to the API specification in the future”.22:2 The ownership check is Trailhead’s own rule. A tool without an owner and an eval suite doesn’t ship.

Table 16.4 — Who owns what in Trailhead’s agent surface

Part Owner Reviewer Gate
Names and descriptions Product (per journey) Content design Eval suite passes; Listing 16.5 passes
Schemas and results Engineering (per team) API review Type check; deterministic tests
Annotations, exposedTo Engineering Security Threat-model review (Chapter 12)
Eval suites QA / ML Product Run on every description or schema change
Agent metrics Analytics Product Weekly report (Table 16.3)
Spec and trial tracking One named engineer Tech lead Release notes reviewed each Chrome milestone

The last row deserves emphasis. WebMCP is a Community Group draft in origin trials, and it changes. Chapter 15 records the churn, and Chapter 17 the open questions. Someone has to read the release notes, watch the issues that affect your tools and send the team’s findings back. Chrome’s origin-trial announcement describes the trial as a way of “gathering user feedback, with the goal of informing future iterations of the API”, and its documentation invites feedback on the API shape in the explainer’s repository and Chromium bugs for implementation problems.2322:3 A company that runs WebMCP in production and never reports what it learned is leaving its influence on the standard unused.

Still in flux: what could change these plans

Who sees your tools. The explainer is considering a native-agent keyword for exposedTo that would control whether the browser’s built-in agent sees a tool, with different defaults for top-level pages and iframes.8:1 That could change how many agents reach your tools without any change on your side. Agent identity and confirmation. The page can’t tell which agent is calling, and the design for asking the user for input during a call (requestUserInteraction() versus requestUserInput(), issues #165 and #204) is unresolved. Chapter 13 tracks both. Budgets. Chrome’s character budgets are provisional and may become limits in the specification.22:4 Tool grouping. Proposals for higher-level “skills” (#161) and for tool collections with progressive disclosure (#255) could change how many tools a page can sensibly expose. On 3 September 2026 the Community Group resolved to “seek explicit model harness creator feedback and defer the tool collections feature”.24 Browser behaviour. In our tests Chromium 156 returned getTools() in alphabetical order, not registration order, and fired toolactivated for in-page calls. Neither is guaranteed, so don’t build reports that depend on them.2:2

Trailhead’s plan on one page

By the end of Monday, Kari’s whiteboard has a plan she can take upstairs.

  1. Release 1: discover and decide. search_products and compare_products, read-only, results rendered in Trailhead’s own grid and comparison table. Measurement and attribution from day one (Listings 16.2–16.4).
  2. Release 2: the cart and the checkout handoff. add_to_cart, get_cart and checkout, with checkout stopping at the summary and the customer’s click placing the order. The confirmation design comes from Chapter 13.
  3. In parallel: the backend MCP server. search_products and get_order_status for assistants that aren’t in the browser, sharing services, names and evals with the page (Chapter 3).
  4. Governance. The catalog file (Listing 16.1) with an owner and an eval suite per tool, the CI check (Listing 16.5), the ownership table (Table 16.4) and one engineer tracking the spec.
  5. Success criteria for the quarter. Tool outcome mix above an agreed ok rate. Assisted orders measured against comparable unassisted sessions. A short list of findings sent back to the Community Group.

None of this needs WebMCP to win the standards debate. The tools wrap code Trailhead already has, the measurement is ordinary analytics and the catalog is good practice for any agent surface, including the backend server. If WebMCP changes shape, the catalog and the evals carry over, and the adapter is the part that changes. Chapter 17 looks at how that adapter might need to change.

Chapter summary

  • WebMCP converts visits you already have. Tools are discovered only during the user’s visit, and there is no central registry. Static manifests were set aside as the primary mechanism, and discovery for sites that aren’t open is an open proposal. Agent-readiness resembles SEO in its need for good machine-facing copy, not in its acquisition power.
  • Choose first journeys by actuation pain, value per completion, code reuse, the cost of a wrong action and the number of tools needed. Search and comparison come first, then reversible cart steps, then a checkout that stops at your confirmation screen. Keep the tool count small.
  • WebMCP keeps the agent a guest on your site: tools run in your tab, update your UI and disappear when the tab closes. It doesn’t stop agents comparing your structured results with competitors’. Show results on the page, return the facts that make you the right choice, keep consequential steps on your page and never over-ask.
  • Every call runs your code, so tools are easy to measure. The page can’t tell which agent is calling: execute receives only the input and a signal, and toolactivated and toolcancel carry only a tool name. Record outcomes (ok, Chapter 11’s four statuses, threw, aborted), codes and durations, not inputs. Attribute orders to agent help by tab session, and treat assisted as different from caused.
  • Pricing and policy decisions surface early: same prices for agents and people, rate limits that allow comparison, terms of service that match the tools you register, human-in-the-loop as policy, evidence for disputes, and untrustedContentHint for user-generated content.
  • Use WebMCP and backend MCP together: one implementation behind two adapters, the same names and schemas where they overlap, and different boundaries where the context differs.
  • Tools are product surface. Copy, schema, evals and security annotations have different owners. Description changes need re-registration and an eval run. Enforce Chrome’s provisional budgets in CI, and give one person the job of tracking the spec and reporting back.

Chapter 17 turns from today’s plan to the open questions (output schemas, streaming and multimodal data, cross-document responses, service-worker tools and the competing futures for the API) and ends with a checklist for building now in a way that survives whichever future arrives.
